bullets: PrincipalBench v2 is a new audit and replacement effort for evaluating the model that coordinates a multi-agent pipeline. Its authors report that version 1 could not support model comparisons: 433 of 500 tasks lacked real questions or reference answers, every episode included a failure, and only three distinct failures were tested. A policy that flagged everything could therefore score perfectly on detection. [E030] Why it matters: If you are choosing an orchestrator—the model that assigns and supervises work—this means version 1 scores should not drive selection. The audit identifies concrete validity checks for any replacement suite: substantive tasks, varied failures, and negative cases where no failure should be reported. [E030] Evidence: E030. Medium confidence.

Journeyman is a new agent benchmark that scores the work process rather than only the final pass or fail. Eight seed-rebuildable simulated jobs test ten behaviors, including repeating ineffective actions, stopping for the right reason, identifying unreachable goals, estimating their cost, and treating planted false information as fact. The simulator can verify claimed actions against its state. [E017] Why it matters: If you are evaluating agents for operational work, a correct final answer can hide wasteful or fabricated intermediate behavior. Journeyman offers a way to compare agents on trace-level conduct without granting them access to real files, making process quality a separate selection criterion from task completion. [E017] Evidence: E017. Medium confidence.

The new Headroom Decision Procedure package formalizes a prerequisite for human-agent protocol experiments: compare against a matched no-protocol baseline and verify that enough improvement is possible to interpret the protocol’s effect. It includes worked tables for opportunity, severity scaling, sensitivity to decision thresholds, paired uncertainty, and scripts that regenerate the examples. [E006] Why it matters: If you are deciding whether a team workflow improves human-agent performance, this procedure helps distinguish an ineffective protocol from a task where the baseline already leaves little room to improve. That changes whether an observed difference can support deployment or further experimentation. [E006] Evidence: E006. Medium confidence.

The Trust-Calibration Benchmark is a new, auditable qualification package for admitting language models to human-computation tasks. It contains 60 yes-or-no items across five domains, audited labels, repeated responses from nine models under three administration protocols, confidence-elicitation and transfer-study data, a 5,700-response cache, and offline analyzers that reproduce the reported results. [E005] Why it matters: If you are using stated confidence to decide when a model may perform or route human work, this package lets you test whether calibration survives protocol changes and transfers beyond the initial items. Its cached responses and offline analysis also reduce dependence on changing model endpoints when reproducing an admission decision. [E005] Evidence: E005. High confidence.

ReconRAG is a new benchmark and code release for retrieval-augmented generation, where a model answers using retrieved documents, when regulations change over time. It reconciles amendments and replacements at ingestion and provides 57 Indonesian regulation pairs, 418 validated questions, frozen prompts, graded answers, human labels, and code that reproduces the paper’s tables. [E012] Why it matters: If you are selecting a system for regulatory question answering, ordinary retrieval accuracy does not show whether it cites the version that was legally in force. ReconRAG adds version reconciliation as a measurable requirement, allowing architectures to be compared on amendment-aware answers rather than document matching alone. [E012] Evidence: E012. High confidence.

A new biomedical-waste benchmark study directly addresses duplicate leakage: pre-augmented image collections can place transformed copies of the same source photograph in both training and test sets, allowing memorization to inflate measured accuracy. The study evaluates classification with duplicate-aware splitting and connects predictions to disposal safety. [E023] Why it matters: If you are evaluating image classifiers on datasets distributed with rotations or other transformed copies, a random split may not measure performance on genuinely unseen photographs. This artifact supports making source-image grouping part of the split design before using accuracy to choose a model for waste segregation. [E023] Evidence: E023. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: PrincipalBench v2 是一项新的审计与替代工作，用于评估负责协调多智能体流水线的模型。其作者报告称，版本 1 无法支持模型比较：500 项任务中有 433 项缺少真实问题或参考答案，每个回合都包含故障，并且仅测试了三种不同的故障。因此，一项将所有情况都标记为故障的策略可以在检测上获得满分。[E030] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择一个编排器——即分配和监督工作的模型——这意味着版本 1 的分数不应作为选择依据。该审计为任何替代评测套件明确了具体的有效性检查：有实质内容的任务、多样化的故障，以及不应报告任何故障的负例。[E030] Evidence: E030. Medium confidence.

Journeyman 是一个新的智能体基准，评估工作过程，而不只是最终通过或失败。八项可从种子重新构建的模拟工作测试十种行为，包括重复无效操作、基于正确理由停止、识别无法实现的目标、估算其成本，以及将预先植入的虚假信息当作事实。模拟器可以根据自身状态核验智能体声称执行的操作。[E017] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估用于运营工作的智能体，正确的最终答案可能掩盖浪费资源或捏造的中间行为。Journeyman 提供了一种在轨迹层面比较智能体行为的方式，同时无须授予其访问真实文件的权限，从而使过程质量成为独立于任务完成情况的选择标准。[E017] Evidence: E017. Medium confidence.

新的 Headroom Decision Procedure 软件包将人机协作协议实验的一项先决条件形式化：与匹配的无协议基线进行比较，并验证是否存在足够的提升空间，以便解释协议的效果。它包含针对机会空间、严重程度缩放、对决策阈值的敏感性、配对不确定性的示例表格，以及可重新生成这些示例的脚本。[E006] Why it matters: 如果你正在判断某种团队工作流能否改善人机协作表现，这套流程有助于区分无效的协议与基线已几乎没有提升空间的任务。这会改变观察到的差异能否支持部署或进一步实验的判断。[E006] Evidence: E006. Medium confidence.

Trust-Calibration Benchmark 是一个新的、可审计的资格评估软件包，用于判断是否准许语言模型承担人类计算任务。它包含横跨五个领域的 60 个是非题、经审计的标签、九个模型在三种施测协议下的重复回答、置信度引导与迁移研究数据、一个包含 5,700 条回答的缓存，以及可复现所报告结果的离线分析器。[E005] Why it matters: 如果你使用模型所陈述的置信度来决定何时可让模型执行或分派人类工作，该软件包可用于测试校准效果能否经受协议变化，并迁移到初始题目之外。其缓存回答和离线分析还可降低复现准入决策时对不断变化的模型端点的依赖。[E005] Evidence: E005. High confidence.

ReconRAG 是一个面向检索增强生成的新基准及代码发布，针对法规随时间变化时模型利用检索到的文档作答的场景。它在摄取阶段对修订与替代关系进行校正，并提供 57 对印度尼西亚法规、418 个经验证的问题、冻结的提示词、带评分的答案、人工标签，以及可复现论文表格的代码。[E012] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择用于法规问答的系统，普通的检索准确率无法表明系统引用的是否为当时具有法律效力的版本。ReconRAG 将版本校正纳入可衡量要求，使不同架构能够基于具备修订感知能力的答案进行比较，而不仅仅比较文档匹配。[E012] Evidence: E012. High confidence.

一项新的生物医学废弃物基准研究直接处理了重复数据泄漏问题：预先增强的图像集合可能会将同一源照片的变换副本同时放入训练集和测试集，从而使记忆效应夸大测得的准确率。该研究采用可感知重复项的数据划分来评估分类，并将预测结果与处置安全联系起来。[E023] Why it matters: 如果你正在使用包含旋转图像或其他变换副本的数据集评估图像分类器，随机划分可能无法衡量模型在真正未见过的照片上的表现。该成果支持在使用准确率选择废弃物分类模型之前，将按源图像分组纳入数据划分设计。[E023] Evidence: E023. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: The Federated Governance Benchmark Dataset v1.0 (FGBD) is a reproducible synthetic benchmark dataset for evaluating governance latency, review complexity, evidence coverage, escalation behavior, approval workflows, and control coverage across simulated federated enterprise operating models. The dataset contains 10,000 programmatically generated synthetic governance records representing centralized, federated, and hybrid operating models under controlled benchmark conditions including low latency, high review complexity, missing evidence, escalation, policy exceptions, cross-business-unit coordination, and conflicting control requirements. The dataset is designed for research and benchmarking of enterprise AI governance, decision intelligence, governance operating models, control effectiveness, auditability, and workflow analysis. Derived metrics are calculated from documented underlying fields using deterministic rules. All records are synthetic and were generated programmatically using a fixed random seed for reproducibility. The dataset contains no customer, employee, patient, financial-account, government, or production enterprise records and does not represent observations from real organizations.

evidence_items.summary: Purpose Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real-time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. Acquisition and validation methods The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI-linear accelerator (MRI-linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open-source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Data format and usage notes The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient-specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030. Potential applications The DoseRAD2026 dataset enables benchmarking and development of fast dose calculation methods for radiotherapy applications.
evidence_items.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI‐accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy

evidence_items.summary: The Trust-Calibration Benchmark (TCB): 60 yes/no items across five domains with gold labels and a per-item label audit, per-trial responses of nine models under three administration protocols, repeated-sampling, confidence-elicitation manipulation and transfer-study data, cached LLM responses, analyzers that reproduce every number in the paper offline, and the camera-ready paper materials. Adds the 54-item computable-gold battery used in the transfer study and the full 5,700-entry response cache from the project folder. Dataset accompanying the paper Qualification by Calibration: A Readable Benchmark for Admitting Language Models to Human-Computation Tasks, 2026 ACM Conference on Human-AI Complementarity and Alignment (HCOMP 2026) (https://doi.org/10.1145/3834580.3838735). Paper abstract. When several language models are wired together into a human-computation pipeline, the system routes, arbitrates, and escalates work according to how confident each model says it is, so a team builder needs a way to screen candidate models the way crowdsourcing has long screened human contributors: with a small, inspectable qualification test. We present such an instrument, a compact battery of yes-or-no questions across everyday domains on which a model reports an answer and a confidence, with every gold label independently audited. Our central contribution, however, is the audited harness and the interface properties it measures, not accuracy discrimination: qualification verdicts for model workers are only as valid as the harness that administers them. Evaluating a diverse panel of contemporary models under three administration protocols, we show that a naive harness, with a fixed token budget and an unaudited parser, manufactures failing workers out of competent ones, misreading a model that answers essentially every item correctly as badly inaccurate, answer-biased, and overconfident.

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic worked example for the headroom decision procedure: worked-headroom, planning-headroom, severity-scaled and guard-sensitivity result tables, and the scripts that generate them. Dataset accompanying the paper Headroom Before Protocol Effects: A Decision Procedure for Human-Agent Evaluation, Human-AI Coevolution Workshop (HAIC) at NeurIPS 2026 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=odOgsQYleZ). Paper abstract. A team protocol has no interpretable benefit without a matched no-protocol baseline and decision-relevant headroom. We present a reporting method that tests admissibility, identifies the marginal contrast, evaluates opportunity, and maps paired uncertainty to an operational action. It distinguishes exact headroom on a fixed battery from uncertain population headroom used in planning. A published meta-analysis of human-AI experiments illustrates why the estimand matters: the same evidence supports augmentation relative to humans alone but contradicts synergy relative to the better constituent. Neither comparison identifies a coordination protocol without a matched no-protocol team. An executable synthetic application further shows that a promising point estimate can remain operationally unresolved once paired uncertainty is considered, and that near-perfect pilot performance does not by itself make a modest benefit impossible. Several inherited multi-model summaries fail the method's artifact gates, so they do not validate it. This is a bounded position and reporting contribution rather than an adoption-ready standard. Human-facing claims still require direct human outcomes, and we introduce no new human experiment. Known limitations. All tables are synthetic illustrations; the five earlier pilots audited in the paper have no retained raw data. evidence_items.summary: TREAT (Theorem Recognition under Equivalence-preserving mAthematical Transformation): transformed theorem statements with theorem identity metadata and validation fields, theorem-level catalogs and a canonical formula pool, a fixed 960-item evaluation panel, the frozen 2,456-page Wikipedia source snapshot, schemas, checksums and reproducibility materials. Dataset accompanying the paper TREAT: Evaluating Access to Formal Knowledge across Equivalent Mathematical Representations , 28th International Symposium on Symbolic and Numeric Algorithms for Scientific Computing (SYNASC 2026) ( https://synasc.ro/2026/ ). Paper abstract. AI systems increasingly operate between flexible input representations and formal objects used by downstream tools. A key challenge is recognizing when an unfamiliar formulation denotes a known formal object. We study this challenge through theorem recognition: given an equivalence-preserving transformation of a theorem condition, a model must recover the theorem identity associated with the standard statement. We introduce TREAT, a benchmark designed to isolate this representation-dependent access problem. Rather than paraphrasing theorem text, TREAT changes the mathematical form of theorem conditions themselves, expressing known results through residual equations, witness statements, optimization identities, set relations, operator forms, and proof-intermediate characterizations. Starting from scraped theorem pages, we filter for entries with usable mathematical expression forms, extract canonical theorem conditions, and generate transformed variants with recorded assumptions and inverse mappings. The final corpus contains 737 theorem identities and 29,900 transformed rows. On a test panel, the best model retrieves the correct theorem identity in only 60.73% of cases. Other systems reveal different failure modes, including abstention, wrong-theorem commitments, and malformed structured outputs.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Fuzzy decisions may vary with measurement errors and admissible benchmark choices, including thresholds, weights, membership shapes, and aggregation rules. Existing fuzzy uncertainty representations and post-hoc sensitivity analyses do not generally certify decision invariance under their joint variation. This study proposes Benchmark-Multiverse Robustness-Certified Fuzzy Learning (BM-RCFL), integrating benchmark-conditioned fuzzy inference, conservative class-score bounds, object-level robustness certification, fragility diagnostics, and safe benchmark pruning. The evaluated implementation uses a fixed prototype-based reference model rather than end-to-end certificate-aware training. On synthetic data, BM-RCFL achieved an accuracy of $$1.0000$$ , a mean certified radius of $$0.3538$$ , and a certified decision rate of $$99.29\%$$ at $$\rho i \ge 0.20$$ . On a Statistics Indonesia welfare panel with constructed reference classes, reference agreement was $$0.6404$$ , the mean certified radius was $$0.2028$$ , and $$57.02\%$$ of cases met the same threshold. No sampled perturbations within the certified regions changed decisions, providing an empirical implementation-consistency check rather than a mathematical proof. Full-enumeration verification using the same conservative bounds produced identical certificates, while benchmark pruning accelerated certification by factors of $$1.93$$ and $$3.14$$ on the respective datasets. Adversarial search identified decision reversals beyond the certified regions, and sensitivity analyses demonstrated dependence on benchmark widths and perturbation-metric scaling. BM-RCFL therefore provides an interpretable, assumption-dependent decision-stability assessment rather than a guarantee of decision correctness.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable fuzzy decision stability modeling for decision engineering under measurement and benchmark uncertainty

evidence_items.summary: OpenRE-Bench is an open-source benchmarking infrastructure for large language model (LLM) based multi-agent requirements-engineering (RE) frameworks. Such frameworks are increasingly common, but they use different agent roles, negotiation policies, and output shapes, and are typically evaluated on their own runtimes, metrics, and small sets of curated system descriptions, which makes fair, reproducible comparison difficult. OpenRE-Bench addresses this with four reusable pieces: a shared run harness with one input, phase-artifact, and metric contract; an adapter mechanism through which a framework joins by implementing a single adapter, leaving cases, metrics, and other adapters untouched; a reproducible GitHub issue-mining pipeline that grows the corpus from real feature requests; and a versioned case suite. As a demonstration, we mine 3,000 fetched issues across five projects (three languages, five domains) into five cases, package them with five hand-built cases as the compact v1.0 suite, and run three heterogeneous frameworks (MARE and iReDev as paper-faithful reimplementations, plus QUARE) under one protocol. OpenRE-Bench originated as the evaluation back-end of our QUARE study and has since been reused by two further studies of our group. It is released with a pinned environment, a Docker image, frozen API snapshots, a 651-test suite, and the full pool of 1,396 filtered issues behind the mined cases.

evidence_items.summary: Journeyman grades how an agent worked, not whether it passed. It drops an agent into eight small simulated jobs — diagnose a crashed service, assay an alloy at a bench, walk a fogged maze, pick up a night shift from a note that lies — and scores the walk on ten axes: did it keep hitting a wall that had already answered, did it stop when the work's object was served or when the budget ran out, could it name what it could not reach and price it, did it repeat a planted false story as fact. Nothing touches real files; every world is simulated and seed-rebuilt, so a claimed exit never reached is caught by arithmetic. What is unusual is not the grading — it is who is allowed to grade. Calibrating an LLM judge before trusting it is standard advice; almost nobody ships the labels to do it with. Three things follow from taking it literally. The calibration set is inside the package: 82 cases across seven axes, labelled by a three-family council in a blind round and an anonymous evidence-quoted second round, distilled from real agent records rather than synthetic vignettes. A judge that has not passed it cannot score — journeyman qualify grants or refuses a badge, and an unqualified run is stamped NOT COMPARABLE. And the judges that failed are published by name, beside the ones that passed. Two scoring layers, and the boundary between them is enforced. Facts are counted programmatically from the record; the questions no counter can answer go to a pluggable judge, one call per rubric item, with the verdict echoed from a fixed label set. Moving a judgement into a deterministic counter to save a call is a standing prohibition, not a preference. The record of being wrong is shipped with it. The first calibration set taught a lesson that the second retracted: under the earlier questions no judge outside one family read one axis at threshold, and that looked like a finding about judging skill. Under the revised definition every judge screened passes it.
evidence_items.title: Journeyman: a process-quality benchmark for LLM agents

evidence_items.summary: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.
evidence_items.title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Machine-learning approaches for soil moisture modelling are expanding rapidly, but their comparison remains difficult because studies often use different target data, predictors, preprocessing methods, and evaluation strategies. Here we present SoMoBench, a quasi-global benchmark dataset that provides standardised predictor inputs and soil moisture targets for data-driven modelling. The targets are derived from in situ observations provided by the International Soil Moisture Network and Brazil’s CEMADEN network. Sub-daily measurements are aggregated to daily values and assigned to a common 0.25° grid for three nominal soil layers (0–10, 10–30, and 30–50 cm). To reduce site-dependent offsets while retaining observation-derived temporal variability, each station series is adjusted to the mean and standard deviation of collocated ERA5 soil moisture. Target series are constructed only for grid cells containing at least one eligible station, and no spatial interpolation is applied. For each grid cell and layer, the longest station record is used as the primary series, and temporal gaps are filled with validated secondary-station record from the same grid cell when available. The current release spans 2001–2024 and includes 1,445 grid cells with at least one target layer, along with daily ERA5 meteorological predictors for 2000–2024. We characterise the spatial and temporal properties of the targets and illustrate their use with climatology-based and Ridge regression models. The release also includes a Python example notebook and baseline performance results to support reproducibility. SoMoBench is designed as a reusable community resource for observation-informed benchmarking and model intercomparison in soil moisture modelling. The dataset is available for peer review through Zenodo; access information is provided in the Data availability section.
evidence_items.title: SoMoBench: a quasi-global benchmark dataset for data-driven soil moisture modelling with in situ-derived targets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Image-based artificial intelligence models for pediatric fracture localization may exploit demographic signals that are correlated with fracture distribution. Quantifying the discrimination available from demographic metadata alone provides a reference for interpreting image-only and multimodal models. Methods We performed a secondary analysis of the open PediURF dataset, preserving its original patient-level training (n = 4,212) and test (n = 1,053) split. Only age and sex were used as predictors. Logistic regression (LR), Gaussian naive Bayes, radial-basis-function support vector machine, random forest, and gradient boosting were tuned exclusively in the training set. Standard training, inverse-frequency cost-sensitive training, and a post hoc equal-prior decision rule applied to standard LR were compared. The primary discrimination measure was macro one-vs-rest ROC-AUC. Test uncertainty was quantified with 2,000 bootstrap resamples. Paired ΔAUC comparisons were Holm-adjusted. Calibration, class-specific recall, and a training-estimated saturated age-by-sex reference were also evaluated. A test-label-derived saturated model was reported only as an optimistic empirical oracle reference, not as a deployable or theoretical upper bound. Results Among 5,265 children with confirmed fractures, 64.1% were distal, 25.1% midshaft, and 10.9% proximal. Standard LR achieved a test macro AUC of 0.704 (95% CI 0.674–0.734), comparable with the training-estimated saturated reference (0.698). Random forest (0.701) and gradient boosting (0.699) were within the prespecified analytic equivalence framework relative to LR, whereas SVM was lower (0.648; ΔAUC − 0.056; Holm-adjusted p < 0.004). Standard models had poor proximal-class recall. Cost-sensitive training increased proximal recall to 0.450 for most algorithms but worsened probability calibration.
evidence_items.title: Demographic Baseline for Pediatric Forearm Fracture Localization: A Machine- Learning Benchmark Using the PediURF Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Improper segregation of biomedical waste allows infectious and otherwise hazardous material to enter general waste streams, with consequences for public health and the environment. Reliable automatic classification at the point of generation could support safer segregation and disposal. Deep learning has been applied to this task, but the public image datasets used for training and evaluation are commonly distributed in a pre-augmented form, in which each source photograph appears as many transformed copies. A conventional random train–test split then places near-identical copies in both sets, so the reported accuracy partly reflects memorisation rather than generalisation. We study automatic classification of 23 biomedical waste categories (15,600 background-removed images) with explicit attention to this issue. Because the dataset carries no ground-truth labelling of duplicates, a leakage-free partition cannot be certified; instead, visually near-identical images are grouped from image content using ORB keypoints with RANSAC geometric verification and kept within a single split, and this controlled estimate is compared against the fully mixed random split, which is known to be leaked, as an optimistic reference. Across four transfer-learning backbones, ConvNeXt-Tiny performs best, reaching a macro-F1 of 0.847±0.007 under the controlled split against 0.958±0.003 under the random split, so naive evaluation is optimistic by about eleven points. Mapping the categories onto World Health Organization hazard streams yields a disposal-bin accuracy of 0.892, with 1.76% of hazardous items misrouted to general waste. The study offers a benchmark and a more realistic basis for reporting automatic biomedical-waste classification.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Ocean salinity is an Essential Ocean Variable that underpins our understanding of Earth’s climate system and the global hydrological cycle. Reliable and accurate salinity observations are therefore critical, yet historical profile archives contain heterogeneous data quality, and the community lacks benchmark-based recommendations for salinity automatic quality control (AutoQC). Under the International Quality-controlled Ocean Database (IQuOD) framework, we developed a benchmark-based approach to compare suites of salinity AutoQC tests from seven international oceanographic institutions. The suites comprised 30 individual checks and were evaluated based on several manually (expert) quality-controlled benchmark datasets. We assessed ~6,400 QC configurations in receiver operating characteristic (ROC) space and identified three best-practice schemes for distinct user priorities. These comprised a high-detection scheme with a high true-positive rate (HTPR), a conservative scheme with a low false-positive rate (LFPR), and a balanced scheme with a cut-off between HTPR and LFPR. We further examined their spatial and vertical performance and investigated factors underlying their contrasting behaviour, with local climatological range check and the constant-value checks accounted for most between-scheme differences. This result suggests that regional salinity structure, observational sampling density, and threshold design may strongly affect the trade-off between detecting erroneous observations and retaining valid data. Our results provide a transparent framework for salinity AutoQC best-practice recommendations while highlighting where an additional regional and depth-dependent validation remains necessary.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-based assessments of best-practice automatic quality control for ocean salinity in-situ observations

evidence_items.summary: Agentic systems operating in adaptive automation environments require persistent memory to retain past actions, qualify outcomes, and improve performance over time. Existing memory mechanisms are architecturally diverse but evaluated in isolation using inconsistent benchmarks, limiting direct comparison. This scoping review systematically examines twelve state-of-the-art memory systems across four architectural categories: Structured Memory, Long-Term Memory, Short and Long-Term Memory, and Workflow and Procedural Memory. Eleven of the twelve are evaluated empirically across nine benchmark datasets spanning conversational question answering, long-document comprehension, and agentic task execution. Memory3 is surveyed but not evaluated, because its memory is built into the model through pre-training and cannot be run on a shared frozen backbone. Every system is evaluated on the datasets aligned to its architectural category, using the same GPT-4o-mini backbone, the same metrics, and the same decoding settings. We also run the backbone with no memory at all, which gives a floor against which each system’s contribution can be measured. Results show that no single architecture dominates all task types. Mem1 leads Contains-Match on conversational tasks while MemoryOS leads Token F1 on the same group, ReadAgent leads multiple-choice long-document comprehension and A-Mem leads open-ended long-document generation, and AWM beats AgentFly on all workflow-level tasks. Measured against the no-memory floor, memory helps a great deal on long-document benchmarks but adds little on multi-hop factoid retrieval, where several systems actually score below the backbone answering from its own pre-trained knowledge. We also identify a verbosity confound.
evidence_items.title: Memory Mechanisms for Agentic Systems in Adaptive Automation: A Comparative Evaluation of Recent Advances (2021–2026)

evidence_items.summary: Differential expression (DE) methods for bulk RNA-seq differ in their statistical assumptions, input data requirements, and supported study designs. Large language model (LLM) agents can automate DE analysis, but they may default to popular methods without checking whether these methods are appropriate for the data. We introduce DE-Rigor-Agent, an assumption-aware agent that organizes DE analysis into three stages: input standardization, method filtering, and method execution. Before executing any DE method, the agent uses expert-curated criteria and dataset-specific diagnostics to evaluate six commonly used methods, documents the reasons for retaining or excluding each method, and executes all retained methods. We evaluated DE-Rigor-Agent on 140 simulated datasets spanning 14 challenging scenarios involving small sample sizes, zero inflation, expression outliers, pre-normalized inputs, and confounded batch effects. Benchmarks showed that method-dataset incompatibilities could lead to inflated false discovery rates (FDRs) or reduced statistical power. Two general-purpose LLM agent baselines, including one explicitly prompted to consider statistical assumptions, selected DESeq2 or edgeR for nearly all datasets. In contrast, DE-Rigor-Agent's filtering decisions closely matched the incompatibilities introduced in the simulations and remained consistent across random seeds, with little additional computational cost. These results demonstrate that DE-Rigor-Agent provides an automated approach to assessing method suitability, making DE analysis more rigorous and transparent.
evidence_items.title: DE-Rigor-Agent: An Agentic Workflow for Assumption-Aware Differential Expression Analysis of Bulk RNA-seq Data

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems place a principal model in charge of decomposing work, supervising worker agents, and synthesising their outputs, yet orchestrators are still chosen with benchmarks that measure single-model task performance. PrincipalBench was introduced to measure orchestration directly. This report describes its second version. We first audit the v1 release against its own code and data and find that it cannot support model comparisons: 433 of its 500 tasks are templated placeholders without real questions or gold answers, every evaluation episode contained an injected failure so a policy that flags everything attains perfect detection, only three distinct failures were ever injected, the context-coherence metric was computed from worker outputs and is therefore identical for every model, and two-thirds of injected failures came from a different domain than the task. A model-free "flag everything" policy scores 0.52 PrincipalScore under the v1 harness. PrincipalBench v2 replaces the protocol with a two-phase sealed design: planning is scored from the question alone; supervision is scored on gold-aligned worker reports in which half of the episodes are clean controls and failures are derived from the hop's own gold output. Detection is chance-corrected (Youden's J), the final step is withheld so the orchestrator must synthesise the answer, and coherence is measured on the orchestrator's own ledger. The v2 core split contains 67 hand-authored tasks (289 subtasks, 335 episodes over five seeds). Reference policies now behave as a benchmark should: degenerate strategies score 0.00 on detection and at most 0.50 PrincipalScore, while only a full oracle reaches 1.00. We withdraw the model rankings reported with v1 and release v2 as the basis for future, reproducible orchestrator evaluations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KalarisLabs/Principal-Bench.
evidence_items.title: PrincipalBench v2: A Validity-First Benchmark for LLM Orchestrators in Multi-Agent Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: Automated video capsule endoscopy (VCE) classification remains challenging due to severe class imbalance, limited source-video diversity, and variations in image appearance across datasets. Although deep learning models have demonstrated promising performance on established benchmarks, their reliability under different validation protocols and external dataset shift remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce DMSNet, a deformable adaptive multi-scale edge-guided attention network integrating adaptive multi-scale feature fusion, deformable lesion refinement, edge-guided attention, and sparse feature selection. We benchmark DMSNet against 18 representative convolutional, transformer-based, and pretrained vision architectures on Kvasir-Capsule under random frame-level and source-video-disjoint validation protocols. We further identify source-video overlap between the original training and test splits and evaluate model performance on both the complete test set and a source-video-disjoint subset. Under random frame-level validation, DMSNet achieves an MCC of 0.442 $\pm$ 0.020 on complete test set and 0.456 $\pm$ 0.037 on the source-video-disjoint subset. On the external CV2024 dataset, ConvNeXt-Tiny achieves the highest MCC of 0.207, while performance degrades substantially across architectures relative to in-domain evaluation. We further investigate source-video diversity using a per-class cap of 200 training frames. With the total training-set size held fixed, increasing the maximum source-video coverage from four to eight improves MCC for 17 of 19 evaluated architectures. Overall, these findings demonstrate that model rankings and classification performance depend substantially on evaluation protocol, training-source diversity, and cross-dataset shift, emphasizing the need for source-aware validation and rigorous external evaluation of VCE classification systems.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Evaluation for Video Capsule Endoscopy: Validation Protocol, Source-Video Diversity, and Cross-Dataset Shift

evidence_items.summary: Companion deposit for the conference paper "One Coefficient Is Not Enough: A Pre-specified Replication of the Impostor-Practice Effect on the CMU Keystroke Benchmark" (accepted at AICSET 2026). Killourhy and Maxion (RAID 2010) summarised impostor practice on the CMU benchmark as a single additive coefficient of +1.1 percentage points of equal-error rate in the no-update regime. This deposit re-runs their factorial design without updating — three detectors (scaled Manhattan, outlier count, Mahalanobis nearest neighbour), four training amounts, three feature sets, 51 subjects — and evaluates each of the 36 cells on 16 impostor windows spanning the eight sessions: 576 evaluations. It contains the analysis script, the result file from which every number in the paper is taken, three earlier independent reproductions that the script must match within 1e-12 before reading any cell, the pre-specified protocol (in French, validated on 13 October 2026 before measurement; dated but not lodged in a public registry), and the figure script. The computation is deterministic; a re-run reproduces the result file byte for byte. The CMU benchmark itself is NOT redistributed here. MANIFEST.tsv lists every file with its size and SHA-256; verify manifest.py recomputes them. See README.md for the two documented differences from the internal working copies (identifiers in the protocol and the protocol file name recorded by the script; no numerical value differs). Version 1.1 adds the post-hoc sensitivity analyses reported in Section 4.6 and Table 3 of the camera-ready paper (src/km grid sensitivity.py and results/km grid sensitivity.json): a 200 000-resample bootstrap with five seeds, the unpruned-ROC EER, a random practice slope per subject, a paired-difference model, and a comparison with the predictions of Killourhy and Maxion (2010, Table 1). They were decided after peer review and amend no pre-specified reading.
evidence_items.title: Impostor practice on the CMU keystroke benchmark: code, results and pre-specified protocol for a replication of Killourhy and Maxion (2010)

evidence_items.summary: Automated hate speech detection has advanced considerably for high-resource languages, but the availability of manually annotated resources for Hausa remains limited. This study presents HausaHateData, a multi-source corpus of 6,509 unique Hausa-language text instances collected from Twitter, Facebook, the AfriHate corpus, and other publicly available sources. Each instance was assigned a binary label of hate speech or non-hate speech. Trigger-word annotations were added to hate-speech instances where a relevant word or phrase could be identified, and all instances were assigned a positive or negative sentiment label. Two annotators independently labelled the data, producing an observed agreement of 82.99% and a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of approximately 0.65 before disagreements were resolved through discussion. The final corpus contains 2,565 hate-speech instances (39.41%) and 3,944 non-hate-speech instances (60.59%). To establish benchmark results, XLM-RoBERTa-Large, AfriBERTa and multilingual BERT (mBERT) were fine-tuned for binary classification. At the reported final epoch, mBERT achieved the highest accuracy (96.08%) and precision (98.73%), while AfriBERTa achieved the highest recall (94.15%), F1-score (94.89%) and ROC-AUC (0.977). XLM-RoBERTa-Large recorded an accuracy of 94.93% and an F1-score of 93.25%. These results provide initial benchmark evidence for Hausa hate-speech classification and demonstrate the potential value of HausaHateData for further research on low-resource African language processing. The experimental split and confusion-matrix values should be confirmed against the original prediction files before publication.
evidence_items.title: HausaHateData: A Manually Annotated Multi-Source Dataset for Hausa Hate Speech Detection with Benchmark Evaluation Using XLM-RoBERTa-Large, AfriBERTa and mBERT

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Kernel-level rootkits subvert the operating system to conceal the network ports through which they maintain covert channels, and cloud tenants who cannot access the hypervisor have few reliable defences. Existing detectors stop at a verdict, leaving investigation and response to human analysts and admitting a window during which an active rootkit persists. This paper presents an agentic AI framework that both detects and autonomously responds to kernel rootkits through port-level behavioural analysis. On cloud guests hosted on Google Cloud Platform, a kernel-mode Port Enumerator and a user-mode Port Monitor produce cross-view port lists whose discrepancy, formalized here as a temporal behavioural signal, is classified by a deep ensemble of CNN-LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Autoencoder and GAN. The resulting Rootkit/Benign verdict is handed to an LLM Agent Orchestrator that executes an autonomous perceive-plan-act-reflect loop, invoking security tools under human-in-the-loop oversight for high-impact actions. A second evidence channel is released with the paper as a labelled concealment matrix of 87 kernel rootkit samples described by a binary vector over a 968-entry dictionary of concealed objects, each carrying the technique it uses to hide. We give a mathematical model of the cross-view signal, the fused decision, and the agent’s utility-driven action selection. Evaluated on a Windows Server 2025 guest, the framework detects rootkits with a mean detection latency of 1.2 s while autonomously triaging confirmed threats; on the released concealment matrix the technique of a confirmed rootkit is recovered from its hook vector at 0.846 accuracy against a 0.713 majority-class rate, with the three-way distinction among inline, SSDT and IAT concealment still limited by class imbalance. The response layer is specified and instantiated but not yet measured; Section 5.6 states the protocol by which it will be tested.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Framework for Autonomous Cross-View Kernel Rootkit Detection and Response in Cloud Environments

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.
evidence_items.title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Wildfires represent a critical ecological and socio-economic challenge in Canada, where vast boreal forests and a warming climate have amplified the frequency and severity of extreme fire seasons. Predicting next-day wildfire spread can support fire management, but requires capturing complex interactions among weather, fuels, and terrain. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach to learning these relationships from heterogeneous environmental data, yet its development and evaluation depend on representative datasets. Existing deep learning research on wildfire spread relies predominantly on US-focused datasets, leaving Canadian fire environments underrepresented. To address this gap, we present DailyWildfireCAN, a multi-modal, multi-temporal dataset and benchmark for predicting next-day wildfire spread across Canada. The dataset tracks continuous fire progression over multi-day events at a high spatial and temporal resolution of 90-m and 24-hour, respectively. This resolution preserves fine-scale information relevant to fire-edge geometry, local fuel variations, and terrain effects, supporting research toward improved daily wildfire spread forecasting. DailyWildfireCAN covers 2,440 wildfire events across eight fire seasons 2017-2024 and integrates 33 features across diverse modalities, including topography, meteorology, land cover, vegetation and forest structure, human influence indices, and satellite imagery. We establish a comprehensive benchmark comparing mono-temporal and multi-temporal prediction models, accompanied by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing robustness across wildfire characteristics, geographic regions, and temporal conditions, spatial prediction quality, and sensitivity to reference label variations.
evidence_items.title: DailyWildfireCAN: A Dataset and Benchmark for Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction in Canada

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate SQL and SQL--Python workflows for investment research, but ensuring point-in-time (PIT) validity remains challenging. Agents must enforce disclosure cutoffs and select the appropriate historical states and record versions throughout data retrieval and financial analysis. We introduce \textsc{BuySideFlow}, a benchmark of 408 practitioner-derived Chinese-language tasks spanning equities, funds, fixed income, and macroeconomics over a fixed snapshot from a licensed production financial database. We provide executable references and a taxonomy of temporal errors, pairing result checks with expert audits of executed workflows. We evaluate nine agent configurations on all tasks, with result accuracy ranging from 16.2\% to 36.8\%. An audit of 900 runs on 100 shared tasks confirms PIT violations in 193 of the 380 runs that pass result checks (50.8\%), showing that output agreement alone does not establish temporal validity.

evidence_items.summary: Video-editing agents must update dependent timeline state while keeping the project available for manual revision. We study how to divide responsibility between a language model and the editing environment. We present Cassette-Editor, an agent harness in which manual gestures and agent patches share an action language, executor, rulebook, and history. Within the editor's supported domain and authorized scope, the agent language can express the content changes available to manual editing. The model chooses edits; the editor derives dependent changes, checks project invariants, returns localized diagnostics, and maps source evidence to the current timeline. With GPT-6 Luna as released, the full harness satisfied the scored request checks in 92/93 unattended trials across 31 authored requests on two interview documentaries, against 48/93 with basic tools, an internal baseline with restricted actions and reduced execution support. Follow-up experiments provide evidence that dependency maintenance and rule enforcement with its fixes improve completion under targeted conditions. Read-mapping and repair experiments found lower agent effort with edit-aware reads and diagnostic receipts. A complete-system comparison on 50 TVSum videos found greater agreement with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1 23.8 vs. 20.1). Perceptual quality and sustained human-agent editing remain unevaluated.
evidence_items.title: Cassette-Editor: An Agent Harness for Editing Video the Way You Do

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for medical information, but their suitability for pheochromocytoma education remains uncertain. We compared four contemporary LLMs for knowledge accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability. Methods ChatGPT (ChatGPT-5.6 Sol), DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V4 Flash), Gemini (Gemini-3.6 Flash), and Grok (Grok-4.5 Fast) answered 200 pheochromocytoma-related multiple-choice questions across three independent trials. Google Trends and clinician input were used to develop 15 patient-centered questions. Responses were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, JAMA benchmark criteria, and six readability indices. Results Overall knowledge accuracy differed among the four models ( p = 0.0012), with mean accuracy rates of 93.00% for ChatGPT, 91.17% for DeepSeek, 90.50% for Gemini, and 81.67% for Grok. However, after adjustment for multiple comparisons, statistically significant pairwise differences were limited to ChatGPT versus Grok for overall accuracy (adjusted p = 0.0129) and clinical-presentation questions (adjusted p = 0.0088). No significant differences were identified among ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini. Exploratory assessments of 15 patient-oriented questions suggested differences in information quality, transparency, and readability across models. ChatGPT showed comparatively favorable information quality scores, whereas DeepSeek exhibited a more favorable descriptive readability profile. Nevertheless, transparency was limited across all models, and none achieved the recommended sixth-grade readability standard. Conclusion The evaluated LLM-based chatbots demonstrated generally favorable performance on structured pheochromocytoma-related knowledge questions, although statistically significant pairwise differences in accuracy were limited.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of large language model chatbots for pheochromocytoma education: accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support open-ended visual reasoning, yet their behavior in low-resource languages and sustainability-oriented domains remains underexplored. We introduce a controlled English–Bangla plastic-waste VQA benchmark comprising 402 image records derived from 136 base images and 2,412 question–answer pairs across five waste categories and three task types: recognition, visual description, and environmental reasoning. We evaluate GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B zero-shot using task-specific answer-quality metrics, bilingual consistency, and image ablation. Gemini 2.5 Flash yields the highest recognition point estimate, with 93.5% accuracy and 91.3% macro-F1. Across models, English normalized performance exceeds Bangla by 3.78 points on average, with the largest observed gap for environmental reasoning. Removing the image reduces normalized performance by 66.29 points for recognition, 52.89 for description, and 11.42 for environmental reasoning. The smaller environmental-reasoning ablation gap indicates that, in this benchmark, many environmental questions remain partly answerable from linguistic and domain priors. These results show why answer quality alone is insufficient for multilingual multimodal evaluation and motivate reporting cross-lingual consistency and sensitivity to visual evidence alongside conventional metrics.
evidence_items.title: VisText-VLM2Plastic: A Bilingual Benchmark for Visual Grounding and Environmental Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractManaging customer retention across retail credit-card portfolios remains imperative for containing revenue attrition and safeguarding banking profitability. This empirical study benchmarks five supervised classification architectures to identify observed credit-card customer attrition and investigates the internal attribution mechanisms of the top-performing model using explainable artificial intelligence. Utilizing the BankChurners benchmark comprising 10,127 records across 37 encoded inputs under an unresampled 75:25 stratified split alongside training-only repeated five-fold cross-validation, we evaluated model discriminatory efficacy across threshold-dependent and ranking-based metrics. Gradient Boosting demonstrated the strongest empirical performance on the held-out test split (accuracy = 0.960; weighted F1 = 0.959; ROC–AUC = 0.986; average precision = 0.949), detecting 332 of the 407 observed churners (recall = 0.816; precision = 0.925; F1 = 0.867) alongside 75 false negatives and 27 false alarms, whilst Random Forest yielded comparable ranking capacity (ROC–AUC = 0.984; average precision = 0.934) but lower minority-class sensitivity. Across fifteen repeated training folds, Gradient Boosting achieved mean ROC–AUC of 0.989 (SD = 0.002) and an attrition-specific F1-score of 0.886 (SD = 0.009), while SHAP and ELI5 global attributions on held-out records consistently pinpointed total transaction amount, transaction frequency, and revolving balance as the most decisive predictive drivers. These insights indicate that diagnostic customer reviews can be substantively enhanced by monitoring longitudinal utilization patterns, though retrospective associations must not be equated with prospective warning or intervention efficacy.
evidence_items.title: Classifying credit card customer attrition using explainable artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: There is a strong feeling that artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping most human activities, and this is supported by impressive proof-of-concept reports that were published during the last decade. Furthermore, medicine is a prominent candidate for AI development, due to the overload on medical practitioners, and specific features of medical practice including the existence of general guidelines and diagnostic algorithms, development of evidence-based medicine and use of an accurate vocabulary making it highly suited for processing by artificial intelligence models. Thus, the current challenge is not to determine whether the introduction of AI in medicine is beneficial or even acceptable, but to organize this inevitable evolution to optimize benefit and prevent pitfalls. The aim of this paper is to discuss the main challenges that must be met to optimize AI support to medical practice. It is suggested that (i) specific procedures are needed to ensure the reliability, comprehensiveness and availability of medical datasets, (ii) there is a need for specific benchmarks and guidelines to validate AI use with a reliability comparable to that ensured by procedures currently used in medicine and (iii) the selection of an AI model to perform a given task must be examined to achieve an optimal balance between efficiency, feasibility and cost.

evidence_items.summary: Hyperspectral image analysis increasingly depends on large, densely annotated benchmark datasets. A review of widely used benchmarks reveals persistent gaps: an almost complete absence of multi-temporal acquisitions, predominantly controlled acquisition conditions, and sparse semantic annotation. We present a methodological framework that addresses these gaps and lays the foundation for a multi-temporal hyperspectral benchmark. Specifically, we describe (a) data acquisition through two UAV-based hyperspectral surveys over an industrial earthworks site in Germany using a HySpex Mjolnir VS-620 sensor, complemented by in-situ ASD FieldSpec reference spectra and photogrammetric products; (b) a multi-stage processing pipeline that transforms raw push-broom data into georeferenced surface-reflectance mosaics (∼5 cm ground sampling distance, ∼5.5 million pixels, 487 bands); and (c) two complementary strategies for dense semantic annotation: an interactive, prompt-driven image-based annotation tool built on the Segment Anything Model 3 and a spectral-similarity approach based on the Spectral Angle Mapper. Within a human-in-the-loop workflow, the two strategies appear complementary, providing spatial delineation and spectrally consistent labelling across disconnected regions, respectively, and show potential for accelerating dense annotation while supporting semantic consistency.
evidence_items.title: Towards a multi-temporal hyperspectral benchmark: UAV-based acquisition, processing, and semantic annotation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present a systematic benchmark of MACE interatomic potentials for iron–nickel alloys, focusing on structural, elastic, and finite-temperature properties of chemically disordered body-centered-cubic (bcc) and face-centered-cubic (fcc) phases. The reference dataset comprises spin-polarized PBE density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations for special quasirandom structures (SQS) span-&#xD;ning composition, volume, and shear deformation. A system-specific MACE–sqs model trained on this dataset achieves validation errors of 2.0 meV/atom for energies and 24.3 meV/Å for forces. We compare MACE–sqs with several MACE foundation models, including models trained using Hubbard corrections, through equations of state, equilibrium volumes, cubic elastic properties, and&#xD;thermal lattice expansion. MACE–sqs gives the most consistent overall performance for several zero-temperature structural and elastic benchmarks, although its relative performance depends on property and composition and it does not reproduce all experimental elastic trends. In the finite-temperature comparison, no single model is uniformly superior, and MACE–matpes agrees more closely with experiment for some compositions and comparison metrics.&#xD;Finite-temperature calculations yield reasonable thermal-expansion coefficients near 300 K, while deviations at elevated temperatures and for magnetovolume sensitive compositions highlight the limitation of representing magnetic effects only implicitly through the spin-polarized reference data. These results define the tested application domain in which targeted SQS-based training improves&#xD;upon broad foundation models and identify explicit magnetic degrees of freedom and broader configurational sampling as priorities for future development.

evidence_items.summary: Interpersonal head-motion synchrony may differ in interactions involving adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but its value for held-out dyadic classification remains uncertain. We reanalyzed 36 structured conversations involving 72 unique participants: 18 typically developing (TD) speaker-TD listener dyads (TD-TD) and 18 TD speaker-ASD listener dyads (TD-ASD). Four established phase-difference descriptors were extracted from 100 Hz forehead accelerometry. H1 predicted lower synchrony density and higher phase-difference standard deviation (SD) in TD-ASD dyads; Hedges g values were −1.20 and 1.01, respectively. For H2, seven classifier families evaluated with fixed and nested-cross-validation-tuned configurations showed no consistent nonlinear advantage (median fold-averaged AUCs, 0.731–0.815); equivalence between families was not established. For H3, density plus SD and density alone yielded leave-one-dyad-out AUCs of 0.793 and 0.790, vs. 0.765 for all four descriptors; these results do not demonstrate superiority, equivalence, or noninferiority. Synchrony events per speaker peak were less frequent in TD-ASD dyads (0.257 vs. 0.421), while chance-corrected coupling differences remained uncertain. These exploratory findings provide an interpretable, internally validated benchmark for prospective studies of dyadic behavioral decision support, not individual ASD diagnosis.

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: This retrospective benchmark evaluated scores for selecting regions of panoramic tooth segmentations for review. Methods: Three-member U-Net ensembles trained on UFBA-425 were evaluated on 590 held-out images and subsequently on 329 photographed radiographs. The original mixed-granularity pipeline comparison used the calibrated residual ensemble on 100 pediatric images. Cells in a 2 × 4 grid received regional mutual information (MI) scores but shared one whole-image soft Dice confidence (SDC) value. A lower Dice-risk area under the risk–coverage curve (AURC) indicated better ranking against source masks. Interaction tests, quality subset analyses, and prediction-positive sensitivity analyses were post hoc. Image-key bootstrap intervals may be too narrow for patient-level inference because patient independence was unverified. Results: The primary MI-minus-SDC AURC difference was +0.007 (95% confidence interval −0.033 to +0.041), leaving the comparison inconclusive. Subsequent evaluations were exploratory. Analyses of reference-positive cells (containing reference tooth pixels) received co-principal emphasis after outcomes were known. MI had a higher Dice-risk AURC than the replicated SDC in the pediatric main subset (+0.238) and the local SDC in AKUDENTAL (+0.157 residual, +0.134 ResNet18). When 20% of grid cells were reviewed, the mean maximum pixel probability (MSP) captured more error pixels than MI in seven of ten source/model comparisons, including both AKUDENTAL ensembles. On photographed radiographs, the MSP led by 15.73 percentage points for the residual ensemble and MI by 3.66 for ResNet18. For ResNet18, equal weighting of false-positive and false-negative capture favored MSP by 6.59 points. Conclusions: The primary comparison established neither superiority nor equivalence. evidence_items.summary: Background: Clinical research and biobanking workflows require retrieval and redaction of protected health information (PHI) from clinical documents before sharing with sponsors and investigators, often alongside biospecimens. Manual redaction is time-intensive, error-prone, and may increase organizational risk through privacy exposure. Automated redaction tools could reduce human burden, improve completeness, and minimize exposure. Objective: This exploratory pilot study aimed to measure the human time burden of manual document retrieval and PHI redaction across common clinical document types, quantify accuracy based on missed PHI (false-negative) patterns, and benchmark results against a fully automated redaction system applied to the same source documents. Methods: A prospective time-motion and error characterization study with six experienced research staff were performed. Each participant redacted nine documents four discharge reports, four pathology reports, and one lab-results report. Automated time was defined as zero human time, as machine runtime does not represent human effort; missed PHI was measured using the same criteria in both conditions. Results: Six participants each completed nine documents (54 total). Mean manual session time was 058:54. Mean document-level time was ∼0:06:05, excluding Research Electronic Data Capture search (0:00:51) and miscellaneous time (0:00:48). Manual redaction produced 55 missed PHI instances (∼1.02/document); the automated system missed 3 instances across 18 unique documents (∼0.17/document), all medical staff names. Conclusion: Automated redaction was associated with fewer missed PHI instances with no measurable human time burden. These exploratory results suggest automation may reduce privacy risk and eliminate the nonredaction workflow steps comprising nearly 40% of manual session time, supporting further evaluation in biospecimen research and biobanking operations.
evidence_items.title: Time and Accuracy of Manual Protected Health Information Redaction in Biospecimen and Clinical Research Workflows: An Exploratory Pilot Benchmark Against Automation

evidence_items.summary: Durably removing ~10 Gt CO₂ yr⁻¹ by 2050 is widely treated as necessary for meeting Paris temperature goals. I found three problems with the 10-Gt benchmark when I tracked carbon-dioxide-removal (CDR) estimates across 51 sources and analyzed the underlying scenarios from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). First, the citation pathway traces almost exclusively to IPCC reports, but the 10-Gt magnitude did not come from a direct reading of IPCC outputs. The number first appeared in a 2017 news piece as an informal estimate, was declared the 'needed' amount in a 2019 National Academy report, and propagated from there; low-CDR scenarios in both IPCC and independent sources were largely ignored. Second, 10 Gt CO₂ yr⁻¹ is larger than the IPCC ensemble medians, which are themselves CDR-reliant, treating emissions reductions and future removals as interchangeable. In the 6th Assessment Report (AR6) I found CDR magnitude correlated with near-term mitigation pace, and as target temperatures rose, the additional carbon-budget space was, on median, filled by continued emissions rather than by reduced CDR. Third, as CDR estimates moved into NGO and industry sectors, the discourse shifted: language describing CDR changed from conditional (e.g., 'scenarios show') to prescriptive (e.g., 'CDR is necessary'), risk discussion diminished, and CDR type narrowed to durable approaches only, excluding the nature-based methods the IPCC scenarios included. The 10-Gt benchmark is therefore larger than warranted by the underlying scenarios, disconnected from the mitigation choices that produced it, and stripped of the context decision-makers need. With the next IPCC assessment report (AR7) underway, there is an opportunity to build a better CDR discourse. One that connects CDR magnitude to mitigation choices, includes lower-CDR pathways, matches CDR durability to its varied roles, and characterizes feasibility, costs, and risks.
evidence_items.title: How carbon dioxide removal lost its way: tracing the origin and transformation of the 10-Gt durable CDR target

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language model agents increasingly act on the world through tools such as code interpreters, application programming interfaces, search engines, perception modules and robotic planners. Every tool call is an opportunity for failure: the model may choose the wrong tool, write malformed input, misread a returned value, trust an erroneous output, or leave external systems in a half-changed condition after a partial sequence of actions. This paper is a structured, qualitative review of how the literature detects such failures, corrects them and keeps the state of the agent and its environment consistent while doing so. It adapts the feedback-loop model and the loud/silent distinction of Sun et al. (2024) to organise a taxonomy of failures, groups detection methods into execution signals, output verification, model self-assessment, external critics and human oversight, correction methods into retry, repair, reflection, replanning, rollback and escalation, and consistency mechanisms into idempotency, compensating actions, checkpointing, action logging, state verification and memory hygiene. A study-by-study comparison of nine representative works, including 2025–2026 studies, records their methods, benchmarks, findings, limitations and treatment of state consistency. Within the reviewed corpus, explicit error messages are comparatively well exploited, silent failures appear to remain a major open problem, self-correction without external feedback is reported to be unreliable on reasoning tasks, and state consistency receives less attention than detection and correction. The paper closes with recommendations for evaluation and design and an agenda for future research. The review is not exhaustive and reports no new experiments.
evidence_items.title: Failure Recovery in Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents: A Structured Review of Detection, Correction, and State Consistency

evidence_items.summary: This study audits three public datasets commonly framed as evidence about artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and productivity and evaluates a reconstructed Scale-Adaptive Gated Ensemble Framework for AI Adoption and Productivity (SAGE-AIP) on the employee-level dataset. The audit identifies three material measurement limitations: the 145,000-record adoption file has a distribution statistically indistinguishable from Uniform(0,100) and negligible association with its recorded covariates; the country-year “AI productivity score” is an almost exact deterministic function of adoption, automation and output per worker; and recorded AI-tool information in the employee file is strongly associated with work location. Accordingly, the first two datasets are retained for provenance and econometric diagnostics but are not used to support claims of predictive productivity gains. The employee benchmark uses 150 records, two repeats of shuffled three-fold outer cross-validation, two-fold inner tuning, identical data partitions across models, and employee-level paired bootstrap intervals based on 10,000 resamples. The corrected implementation uses nested cross-fitting: Ridge residual targets for each gate-training fold are constructed using only that fold’s training observations. Random Forest achieved pooled RMSE 0.4935; the equal-weight residual ensemble achieved 0.4923; and full SAGE-AIP achieved 0.5024 (MAE 0.3759; R² 0.7683). The paired interval for the SAGE-AIP–Random Forest RMSE difference included zero, while full SAGE-AIP had slightly higher RMSE than the global-gate ablation. The group-stability penalty made a negligible difference. The findings do not establish predictive superiority for SAGE-AIP or a causal effect of AI use on productivity. The contribution is a transparent data-quality audit and a leakage-controlled evaluation of a reconstructed method, with limitations and unresolved provenance stated explicitly.
evidence_items.title: SAGE-AIP: A Scale-Adaptive Gated Ensemble Framework for AI Adoption and Productivity Prediction-A Multi-Dataset Benchmark and Diagnostic Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: As autonomous artificial intelligence agents become more sophisticated and prevalent in enterprise systems, organizations increasingly deploy multiple specialized agents that operate in parallel on shared workflows. This practice creates a new architectural challenge: coordinating concurrent agents while preventing conflicts and preserving system integrity. Agents may generate competing recommendations, pursue misaligned optimization goals, or take actions that violate enterprise governance policies. This paper examines multi-agent orchestration and conflict resolution as a distinct architectural discipline. The study presents a four-layer orchestration model comprising agent decision-making, conflict evaluation, deterministic resolution, and committed execution. It then compares how three contemporary frameworks, LangGraph, LangChain, and CrewAI, implement this model through different abstractions. Four conflict-resolution mechanisms are also examined: priority-based, policy-aligned, consensus-based, and utility-maximizing. Their underlying logic is formalized through three analytical constructs. The first is a policy-compliant utility maximization model. The second is a consensus quorum threshold grounded in established Byzantine fault tolerance theory. The third is a layered orchestration latency model that explains why hierarchical decomposition improves scalability. These formalizations are presented as structural models rather than measured benchmark results. The analysis shows that each framework favors a different coordination style, that each resolution mechanism offers distinct trade-offs between speed, fairness, and governance assurance, and that hierarchical decomposition reduces coordination overhead as the number of agents grows. The paper concludes that coordination challenges introduced by parallel agents are not obstacles but opportunities for architectural sophistication.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration & Conflict Resolution: Solving Coordination Challenges in Parallel Agentic Systems

evidence_items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24179801 . Overall assessment This preprint reports that a subset of chromatin-enriched RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) activate transcription through intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) whose composition partially resembles that of transcription factor activation domains. Using a classic transcriptional reporter assay, the authors show that selected IDRs activate transcription, and that aromatic residues are required for this activity. A particularly strong result is that the characterized composition of activator IDRs was predictive of new activators, including the CTD of Rpb1. Together with the observation that inducible Rbp1-CTD condensates recruit transcriptional machinery, this work supports a model in which the IDRs of RBPs help recruit coactivators. The identified molecular grammar is compelling, and their model can help explain the coupling of transcription and RNA processing. Overall, the novel transcriptional activator role of RBPs is well supported by the data presented, and the more detailed descriptions of methods and data requested below are mainly meant to allow a better evaluation and understanding of the work. Major points 1. The conclusion that splicing changes were not associated with up-regulated genes after RBP overexpression is central to attributing upregulation to transcription. Fig S3 shows only alternative 3' splice site (A3SS) events, described as an example and it is unclear whether other splicing defects were tested (skipped exon, alternative 5' splice site, mutually exclusive exon, retained introns, etc). Moreover, other post-transcriptional effects are not examined. A summary across all event classes and all upregulated genes would test more rigorously whether upregulation is secondary to splicing changes.

A Paired Ablation Study , 4th Workshop on Mathematical Natural Language Processing (MathNLP 2026), EMNLP 2026 ( https://www.carlostoxtli.com/papers/mathnlp2026-which-mathematical-context.pdf ). Paper abstract. Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is challenging because theorem-relevant information is distributed across multiple forms of mathematical context, including definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions. We study which of these contextual signals help a model recover the specific claim supported by the surrounding setup, using 61 main theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains. For each theorem, we redact the result and represent the remaining setup using six context components. A paired ablation design compares full context, six leave-one-out conditions, and six single-component conditions, yielding 793 generated conjectures. Context components were largely complementary: removing one component usually had little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduced expected-theorem alignment. Local Mathematical Objects provided the strongest standalone signal, while Structural Constraints and Conditions produced the largest alignment decrease when removed.

evidence_items.summary: Dataset Description This dataset presents experimental observations and numerical results from the field performance evaluation of a battery-powered walk-behind spinach reaper. The study investigated the effects of forward speed, pulley diameter, and cutting height on cutting efficiency, conveying loss, and reaping efficiency. The experiment comprised 18 treatment combinations, involving three forward speeds (1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 km h⁻¹), three pulley diameters (50.8, 76.2, and 101.6 mm), and two cutting heights (50 and 75 mm). Three observations (R1, R2, and R3) were recorded for each treatment and performance response, resulting in 162 recorded response values. The deposited dataset includes: Original experimental observations and treatment-wise mean values for cutting efficiency, conveying loss, and reaping efficiency. Regression modelling results, including model coefficients and fitted values. Numerical results supporting the optimization of operating parameters. Field-capacity and field-efficiency calculations.
