evidence_items.summary: Outpatient psychotherapy for individuals with severe trauma-related dissociation, including Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID), Other Specified Dissociative Disorder type 1 (OSDD-1), International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11) Partial DID, and complex post-traumatic stress disorder (cPTSD) or borderline personality disorder (BPD) with prominent dissociation, is frequently constrained by limited specialist availability. Although clinical practice guidelines recommend weekly or twice-weekly sessions, community clinics and public health services often space appointments every two to four weeks. During these extended intervals, patients struggle to maintain treatment continuity across shifting dissociative or affectively dysregulated states. Between-session deterioration is driven by three recurring vulnerabilities: state-dependent memory and executive discontinuities across dissociative states, traumatic invalidation triggered by rigid behavioral contingencies, and relational fawning or crisis escalation aimed at securing the clinician's attention. To address this gap, we present a transdiagnostic self-regulation model and an accessible, paper-based inter-session clinical toolkit. Using DID and OSDD-1 as high-acuity compartmentalized exemplars alongside non-amnesic cPTSD and BPD dissociative states, the model integrates the Theory of Structural Dissociation of the Personality, Dialectical Behavior Therapy adaptations, Schema Therapy mode conceptualizations, and Cognitive Evaluation Theory. The protocol uses daily grounding marks strictly as cross-state informational feedback while keeping basic biological care, safety skills, and clinician availability completely unconditional. Two composite clinical vignettes and a 15-to-20-minute session-opening review protocol illustrate how clinicians can bridge extended inter-session gaps safely.

evidence_items.summary: AGHRI is a multimodal dataset for robot perception of humans in agricultural and off-road environments. AGHRI provides synchronized RGB, depth, fisheye, and 3D LiDAR data collected with a compact mobile robot across diverse settings, including strawberry polytunnels, vineyards, footpaths, and farmsides, under variable lighting and weather conditions. AGHRI comprises 65 sequences totalling 27.4 minutes of multimodal robot sensor data, including 138,741 camera image frames and 13,963 LiDAR frames, with 154,002 annotated 2D human bounding boxes, 27,311 annotated 3D human bounding boxes, 454 camera-specific 2D tracks, and 136 3D tracks. The dataset includes challenging multi-person and occlusion-rich interactions and provides frame-level 2D and 3D annotations with consistent human identities to support 2D/3D detection and tracking tasks.The AGHRI dataset is divided into 10 ZIP archives (from dataset part1.zip to dataset part10.zip), each containing multiple data subfolders. Within each data subfolder, the extracted multimodal sensor observations are stored alongside their corresponding annotations and metadata. Sensor calibration files are stored separately in a shared calibration folder (calibration.zip). In addition, an occlusion annotation file (occlusion log.csv) is provided at the dataset root level, together with a dataset summary file (dataset summary.csv) that describes the contents of each data subfolder and indicates the ZIP archive to which it belongs. This organization allows users to selectively download only the ZIP archives relevant to their needs, rather than downloading the entire dataset.AGHRI dataset is accompanied by a set of conversion and utility tools that support common perception workflows/formats, including YOLO, COCO, KITTI, MMDetection, MOT, and ROS 2.

evidence_items.summary: The recent popularity of consumer-grade virtual reality devices has enabled users to experience immersive Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) dances in virtual environments, where ICH is defined by UNESCO as traditions or living expressions inherited from our ancestors. As in real-world choreography, the dancers in a virtual environment should be instructed in how to perform their dance. However, this can be a time-consuming and challenging task with the current Virtual Reality (VR) controllers. To address these challenges, we introduce an innovative choreography system leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate dance creation and presentation in VR. To achieve this goal, we first establish a corpus dataset comprising almost five thousand prompt phrases to describe fundamental movements and formation changes within dance formation choreography. We then leverage an LLM to understand these prompts, thereby comprehending the commands issued by users during the interaction. Based on the understanding provided by the LLM, these prompts are converted into primitive commands that our system can execute. This allows the virtual character to perform corresponding actions to complete the dance formation choreography. We conduct three user studies with 94 subjects to validate the proposed approach. Through user studies, we find that the proposed approach can help users generate high-quality ICH dances regarding human likeness, appropriateness, and operability. evidence_items.summary: Contamination on outdoor substation insulators changes surface reflectance and, after moisture activation, produces nonuniform Joule heating. A single image band therefore provides condition-dependent evidence and can confuse light contamination with illumination variation or material aging. This study presents a multispectral gated cross-attention classifier (MS-GCA) that combines registered red-green-blue (RGB), near-infrared (NIR), and long-wave infrared (LWIR) images. The method employs multiscale modality encoders, shared-parameter iterative cross-attention, reliability gates, spectral-consistency regularization, and entropy-based uncertainty reporting. A physics-guided benchmark containing 6,000 aligned triplets was constructed from 500 distinct insulator geometries under three environmental states and four contamination grades; geometry identities were separated among training, validation, and test partitions. On the 1,200-triplet test set, MS-GCA achieved 96.8% accuracy, 96.7% macro-F1, and 99.2% macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, while requiring 18.6 million parameters and 12.7 ms per triplet. The method exceeded a strong iterative cross-attention baseline by 1.1 percentage points in macro-F1 and retained 91.4% macro-F1 under an eight-pixel residual registration error. These results support multispectral classification as a robust decision-support component for inspection scheduling, while field calibration and prospective substation validation remain necessary before operational deployment.
evidence_items.title: Multispectral image classification algorithm for contamination monitoring of substation insulators

evidence_items.summary: Verifying corporate financial disclosures against the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is a core auditing task in which experts cross-reference disclosures with hundreds of fine-grained regulatory paragraphs: a laborious, costly, and error-prone process that motivates growing interest in large language models (LLMs) as compliance assistants. Yet single-model accuracy remains insufficient for high-stakes use, and naive ensembling is vulnerable to systematic per-model biases that can drag aggregate accuracy below that of the strongest individual annotator. This gap is addressed with a multi-stage framework, supported by a new benchmark of 19,998 IFRS regulation-disclosure pairs comprising 11,161 unanimous multi-LLM labels and 8,837 human annotations on items where the LLMs disagreed. The framework couples a three-stage domain-adapted sentence embedding pipeline (BERT masked language modeling on SEC EDGAR filings, unsupervised TSDAE and SimCSE adaptation, and supervised contrastive alignment) with a learned ensemble classifier that fuses frozen embeddings and LLM probability features from GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro via Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) optimized gradient-boosted trees. On the disagreement set, the ensemble achieves 81.7% weighted F1, exceeding the strongest single LLM by 10.4 points and majority voting by 14.6 points, and outperforms eleven unsupervised aggregation baselines; the retrieval pipeline attains Recall@15 of 45.3% on unseen regulations. The dataset, model checkpoints, annotation platform, and classifier implementation will be publicly released.

evidence_items.summary: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots.txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.
evidence_items.title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping

evidence_items.summary: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.
evidence_items.title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are being explored to deliver health coaching across multiple contexts. However, the quality and safety of chatbot-generated advice is influenced by how prompts are constructed, and prompt design remains inconsistently described in the literature. This scoping review examined how prompt design has been applied and evaluated in AI health coaching chatbots and summarized the study designs, prompt strategies, and outcomes reported across studies. We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidance and searched PubMed, Embase/Ovid MEDLINE ALL, PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published up to October 2025. Eligible studies examined prompt design in large language model–based health coaching chatbots. Data were extracted using a standardized form and synthesized narratively. Twelve studies were included, spanning mental health, medication use, physical activity, and nutrition contexts. Study designs were primarily simulation-based, with few involving real users. Prompt strategies were grouped into structural modifications, prompting techniques, and role-based approaches. Structural modifications, such as increasing specificity and adding constraints, were most common and were reported to improve response quality and clarity. Prompting techniques were reported to improve task performance but sometimes reduced focus or consistency. Role-based prompting influenced tone, specificity, and guideline alignment. Outcomes focused mainly on response quality, with fewer studies assessing safety or user experience and only one evaluating clinical outcomes. Prompt design is a key, modifiable determinant of chatbot performance. However, current evidence is limited by heterogeneous study designs and minimal real-world evaluation. Greater focus on prompt design is needed to improve the quality and safety of AI-delivered health coaching and its real-world impact on health outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Prompt design in large language model health coaching chatbots: A scoping review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Typhoon-induced extreme waves pose severe threats to coastal communities, infrastructure, and maritime operations worldwide. Accurate and rapid forecasting of significant wave height is therefore critical for disaster response. Physics-based numerical wave models provide physically grounded predictions but can be computationally demanding for high-resolution forecasting, while purely data-driven models often struggle with rare, highly non-stationary extreme events. Recent time-series approaches based on large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for long-range forecasting but remain limited in explicitly representing coupled environmental variables and enforcing physically plausible predictions. Here, we develop the Typhoon Wave Large Language Model (TW-LLM), a physics-informed, domain-adapted framework for forecasting typhoon-induced coastal wave height. Building on Time-LLM, TW-LLM introduces cross-variable covariate interaction to explicitly represent dependencies between wave states and environmental forcing, structured domain-informed prompting for semantic conditioning, and a physics-informed training objective that combines magnitude-weighted Huber loss with wind-forcing consistency and temporal-rate constraints. Trained and evaluated using nine years (2017–2025) of hourly observations from eleven coastal buoys in China, TW-LLM achieves root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of ~ 0.15 m for short-term (6-h) forecasts, 0.3 m for long-term (96-h) forecasts, and 0.23 m under extreme typhoon conditions. With an inference time as low as 5 s per forecast, TW-LLM provides a computationally efficient framework for near-real-time coastal wave forecasting and early warning, with potential to enhance coastal resilience to increasingly severe climate-related hazards.
evidence_items.title: Physics-Informed Time‑Series Large Language Model for Extreme Typhoon Wave Height Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Background: The purpose of this study is to assess the ability of generative AI and a refractive surgeon to distinguish post-LASIK Scheimpflug tomography images based on original excimer laser ablation and to recognize untreated corneas. Methods: Corneal tomography Pentacam images from 204 eyes, which included hyperopic ablations, myopic ablations, myopic astigmatic ablations, mixed astigmatic ablations, or untreated eyes, were compiled. These were individually queried in ChatGPT-5.5 using a multiple-choice prompt to obtain a response. A refractive surgeon was also tested on the same 204 corneas. Results: The clinician obtained higher overall accuracy (85.8% [95% CI 80.2–90.3]) compared to ChatGPT, (60.3% [95% CI 53.2–67.1], p < 0.001) and was significantly more likely to answer correctly overall based on McNemar’s test. Additionally, ChatGPT underperformed in the myopia with astigmatism, mixed astigmatism, and untreated categories, with sensitivities of 38%, 6.3%, and 76%, respectively. Conclusions: The overall accuracy of ChatGPT-5.5 did not meet that of the clinician while ability to identify myopic and hyperopic ablation patterns was comparable. Both the AI model and the clinician had decreased accuracy in myopic astigmatism and mixed astigmatism ablation patterns, though the clinician still performed significantly better. Further studies involving alternative AI models, multicenter data, and standardized evaluation protocols are warranted to establish the clinical applicability of these findings.
evidence_items.title: Distinguishing Post-LASIK Ablation Patterns on Corneal Tomography: Comparing Clinician Versus Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Emerging deep technologies create a competitive technical intelligence challenge because technical architectures, performance claims, ecosystem arrangements, and prospective markets evolve before stable adoption evidence is available. This article develops and illustrates a theory-informed, large language model (LLM)-assisted competitive intelligence (CI) process for assessing the disruptive potential of the development and commercialization of emerging quantum error-correction technologies. The process translates concepts from disruptive innovation, architectural innovation, value proposition analysis, and disruptive threat assessment into intelligence constructs, evidence questions, sequential prompt functions, source-validation criteria, and monitoring outputs. Perplexity.ai supported document discovery, organization, comparison, and preliminary synthesis; the authors evaluated sources, classified claims, and made all final interpretations. The process is illustrated through a comparative documentary analysis of Nord Quantique’s multimode bosonic quantum error-correction approach and IBM’s transmon, surface-code, and quantum low-density parity-check-oriented approach. The analysis identifies NQ as a documented architectural alternative that seeks to embed error protection within superconducting resonator modes. Its proposed reduction of error-correction overhead provides a plausible mechanism for changing system-resource requirements and deployment conditions. However, the retained evidence does not establish comparative system level advantage, lower total cost, a validated customer segment, a disruptive foothold, adoption, or incumbent displacement. The article contributes a source-disciplined and monitorable LLM-assisted CI process for emerging deep technologies.
evidence_items.title: A Theory-Informed, Large Language Model-Assisted  Competitive Intelligence Process for Assessing  Competing Quantum Error-Correction Technologies

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) can extract information from unstructured clinical text, but it remains unclear whether their ability to assess current status translates into reliable predictions of longitudinal outcomes. Objective This study aimed to evaluate DeepSeek’s ability to assess baseline clinical and radiographic status in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), its performance in predicting 6-month outcomes, and its interrun reproducibility. Methods This study used a single-center, prospective observational cohort design to conduct a blinded, retrospective evaluation of the LLM. A total of 128 patients with primary KOA were enrolled, of whom 111 (86.7%) completed the 6-month follow-up and were included in the primary analysis. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and a rheumatologist independently assessed KOA diagnoses, baseline Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) scores, and Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading based on the same standardized interview records and imaging reports and predicted 6-month outcomes. The LLM was run independently 3 times. The actual outcomes determined by another senior physician served as the reference, and the results were compared with the physician’s predictions and the persistence model. Results The LLM showed high baseline diagnostic agreement with the physician (105/111, 94.6%) and good agreement on the WOMAC and KL, but 6-month predictions (WOMAC mean absolute error=5.92-6.58; KL exact agreement=74/111, 66.7%-76/111, 68.5%) were worse than those of the physician comparator (mean absolute error=3.86; 96/111, 86.5%) and not superior to those of the persistence model (mean absolute error=5.43). Despite high interrun intraclass correlation coefficients (0.982 and 0.965), exact agreement between runs was poor (35/111, 31.5% and 7/111, 6.3%). Conclusions The evaluated DeepSeek configuration may support structured baseline KOA assessment.
evidence_items.title: Performance of a Large Language Model for Predicting Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in Knee Osteoarthritis: Single-Center Prospective Observational Study

evidence_items.summary: Whole-Region Comprehensive Land Consolidation (WRCLC) faces persistent evaluation bottlenecks in practice: traditional quantitative monitoring captures physical land-cover changes but fails to interpret cross-sectoral policy semantics, whereas manual administrative review suffers from high operational costs, subjective inconsistency, and severe information asymmetry. To address these challenges, this study develops a domain-adapted Large Language Model (LLM) framework for structured preliminary effectiveness assessment of WRCLC, using Guangdong Province as a case study. Following the standardization and integration of multi-source heterogeneous data across county-level units, a domain-specific model is established using a knowledge distillation framework based on a hard-constraint mechanism combined with LoRA fine-tuning. A six-dimensional evaluation system is established to evaluate project progress, factor endowment guarantee, structural optimization, value realization, bottom-line constraints, and regional characteristics. Qualitative and quantitative validation across typical county-level administrative divisions in Guangdong demonstrates high alignment with expert judgment and robust capabilities in contextual narrative generation. Rather than replacing administrative decision-making or expert review, this framework demonstrates the feasibility of generative artificial intelligence as an auxiliary decision-support tool. Operating within a human-in-the-loop governance paradigm, the proposed approach effectively bridges quantitative spatial metrics and qualitative governance semantics, significantly reducing administrative drafting burdens while enhancing process monitoring, compliance review, and adaptive land governance.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model-Oriented Framework for Effectiveness Assessment of Whole-Region Comprehensive Land Consolidation: A Case Study of Guangdong Province

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming electronic design automation (EDA) by enhancing design stages such as schematic design, simulation, netlist synthesis, and place-and-route. Existing methods primarily focus these optimisations within isolated open-source EDA tools and often lack the flexibility to handle multiple domains, such as analogue, digital, and radio-frequency design. In contrast, modern systems require to interface with commercial EDA environments, adhere to tool-specific operation rules, and incorporate feedback from design outcomes while supporting diverse design flows. We propose a versatile framework that uses LLMs to generate files compatible with commercial EDA tools and optimise designs using power-performance-area reports. This is accomplished by guiding the LLMs with tool constraints and feedback from design outputs to meet tool requirements and user specifications. The framework is used to evaluate case studies on operational transconductance amplifiers, microstrip patch antennas, and FPGA circuits.
evidence_items.title: A flexible language model-assisted electronic design automation framework

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for teaching materials development in higher education, yet the distribution of research attention across material types and the educational value of generated resources remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to examine the applications, material categories, benefits, challenges, and research gaps associated with GenAI-assisted teaching materials development in higher education. A systematic literature review synthesized findings from relevant studies, with the reviewed literature identifying 31 studies in one recent review as a key evidence base for understanding current research patterns. The literature indicates that textual and written materials receive the greatest research attention, followed by assessment and evaluation materials and multimedia resources, whereas game-based and gamified materials remain comparatively underexplored. Findings also highlight GenAI’s potential to improve development efficiency and support resource adaptation, alongside persistent concerns about accuracy, bias, ethical use, and pedagogical suitability. This study contributes a structured perspective on the uneven development of research across teaching material types and identifies priorities for strengthening empirical evidence. Future work should evaluate educational effectiveness across diverse learning contexts, advance multimodal material design, and investigate human–AI collaboration to support accurate, pedagogically aligned, and responsible integration into higher education.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Teaching Material Development in Higher Education

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming marketing practices through advanced data analysis and predictive capabilities. This paper examines AI driven marketing, focusing on customer behavior analysis and predictive marketing. It explores how AI technologies help businesses understand customer preferences, identify purchasing patterns, and anticipate future customer actions. The study discusses applications such as customer segmentation, recommendation systems, sentiment analysis, customer churn prediction, and customer lifetime value estimation. It also examines AI applications across commerce, banking, healthcare, travel, hospitality, and social media marketing. The paper highlights potential benefits, including personalization, improved decision making, marketing efficiency, customer retention, and demand forecasting. However, effective implementation requires attention to data quality, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, and technical expertise. Ethical considerations, including transparency, consent, fairness, security, and human oversight, remain essential for responsible AI adoption. The paper follows a conceptual approach based on secondary literature. It concludes that AI can strengthen marketing effectiveness by integrating customer insights with predictive capabilities. Successful implementation requires collaboration between human marketers and AI technologies. This balanced approach can support customer relationships, informed decisions, and sustainable marketing performance.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Customer Behaviour Analysis and Predictive Marketing

evidence_items.summary: Plant stress is one of the primary limitations to crop growth, yield, and quality and can result from various abiotic and biotic stresses, including drought, extreme temperatures, salinity, nutrient imbalance, pathogens, and insect pests. Early detection of plant stress is crucial for enabling timely intervention and preventing potential crop losses. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for automated plant health assessment has gained increasing attention through image-based deep learning and sensor-based machine learning techniques. However, single-modality approaches may have limited capability to capture the complex relationships between plant visual characteristics and environmental conditions. Multimodal AI can address this limitation by integrating complementary information from visual modalities, such as RGB, thermal, multispectral, and hyperspectral imaging, with environmental indicators, including temperature, humidity, soil moisture, light intensity, and weather conditions. In AI-based plant stress assessment, with a particular focus on multimodal data fusion and early stress prediction. AI architectures, data fusion methods, datasets, sensing modalities, and explainable AI (XAI) techniques are examined in detail. Furthermore, key challenges associated with multimodal dataset collection, sensor synchronization, environmental variability, model generalization, computational requirements, and real-world deployment are discussed. Finally, promising research directions, including temporal multimodal learning, edge AI, explainable multimodal models, low-cost sensing technologies, and foundation models for plant science, are highlighted.
evidence_items.title: MULTIMODAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR EARLY PLANT STRESS PREDICTION: A REVIEW

evidence_items.summary: Arid and semi-arid environments are highly vulnerable to potentially toxic element accumulation because low rainfall, high evaporation, dust transport, episodic runoff, irrigation return flow and groundwater salinity can concentrate metals in soil and water. Saudi Arabia provides a distinctive national case because rapid urbanization, agriculture, cement production, wastewater reuse, coastal development and petroleum-related activities occur across contrasting geological provinces. This review critically synthesizes published evidence on heavy-metal and trace-element concentrations in Saudi Arabian soil, sediment, groundwater, surface water, irrigation water, seawater and wastewater-influenced systems. The review follows a structured critical-review approach: peer-reviewed studies were screened for location, matrix, analytical method, concentration data, quality assurance/quality control information, guideline comparison and reported pollution or risk indices. The evidence shows strong spatial heterogeneity. Central-region datasets dominate the literature, whereas northern agricultural areas, western Red Sea coastal-industrial sites, southern wadis and landfill-affected areas, and eastern oil-related and coastal settings remain important but unevenly represented. Reported hotspots include Cd up to approximately 22 mg/kg in industrial soil, elevated Zn in Riyadh playground soils, As up to approximately 0.18 mg/L in well water and Fe up to approximately 1.45 mg/L in well water. Priority elements are As, Cd, Pb, Cr, Ni, Cu, Zn, Fe and Mn. Their interpretation requires matrix-specific guideline comparison, geogenic background assessment, and land-use context. The review identifies carbonate-evaporite aquifers, Arabian Shield-derived sediments, wadi transport, irrigation return flow, industrial emissions, wastewater inputs and petroleum-related activities as interacting controls.
evidence_items.title: Heavy metal contamination in Saudi Arabian soil and water: Regional distribution

evidence_items.summary: Powdery mildew, caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (Bgt), is a major foliar disease of bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.). Genomic prediction (GP) can accelerate breeding for this trait, but conventional, machine-learning (ML), and deep-learning (DL) methods have rarely been compared side by side. Using the Wheat Association Mapping Initiative (WAMI) panel (n = 286), phenotyped for powdery mildew severity over three years (DS1–DS3) and genotyped with the Illumina 90K SNP array, we compared 30 GP models under per-year and genotype-grouped pooled cross-validation. Broad-sense heritability ranged from 0.65 to 0.89. In the pooled, leakage-safe analysis, six Bayesian-alphabet models clustered at the top (r = 0.291–0.299), too close to identify a single best model; partial least squares (PLS) regression was the strongest non-Bayesian model, and elastic net was the strongest ML model within each year. Within-year accuracy under random 5-fold cross-validation was higher (up to r ~ 0.70 in DS2) but may be optimistic, as folds were not stratified by genomic relatedness. Accuracy showed limited, non-monotonic sensitivity to marker density and increased, though not strictly monotonically, with training population size. Leave-one-year-out (LOYO) accuracy was near zero (mean r = 0.009); fitting year as a fixed effect did not improve it, and cross-year genetic correlations were low (0.08–0.15), indicating limited shared genetic control across years. DL results apply only to the architectures and sample size tested. With pooled accuracy near r = 0.30, these models suit within-season prediction in this panel, whereas reliable cross-season application is not supported by the present results and will require broader multi-environment training and/or season-specific recalibration.
evidence_items.title: Genomic Prediction for Powdery Mildew Resistance in Wheat: A Thirty-Model Benchmark of Conventional, Machine-Learning, and Deep-Learning Approaches

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination-detection systems are usually judged by a single headline metric, computed under a benchmark design that determines what that metric can show. This paper’s contribution is not a detection algorithm — structural coherence scoring is established — but a methodology for measuring exactly what a benchmark proves and what it does not, applied to the SAS Multimetric Tribunal: a thirteen-module, GPU-free structural classifier combining lexical, entity-mutation, curvature, logical-inversion, topological-similarity, semantic-drift, entropy, complexity, and surprisal signals via a cascading multiplicative penalty (\(\kappa {D} = 0.56\), \(\kappa {R} = 0.15\)). On a stratified 1,800-pair benchmark (HaluEval-Dialogue, HaluEval-QA, TruthfulQA), the tribunal reaches F1 = 98.99% with zero false positives under an A\(\rightarrow\)A identical-text sanity check. We report this figure and then show, using a format-controlled negative (N1) on the same 1,800 IDs, that it measures format asymmetry between source and response rather than hallucination detection. The tribunal flags 1,569 of 1,800 verbatim correct answers presented alone (87.2%), and in HaluEval-QA scores the correct answer as more anomalous than the hallucinated response. Three further findings follow from the same audit. (i) A per-module analysis shows the tribunal’s seven-module core has no content-sensitive module (prior to the optional R3.1 guard): the one module designed to capture semantic divergence (cre isi) gives the same per-ID score whether the response is byte-identical or completely different. (ii) The 87.97-point advantage of multiplicative combination over weighted averaging reported in v4 is an artifact of threshold calibration; under per-scheme thresholds on format-matched negatives, both schemes converge to F1 \(\approx 0.69\) and the multiplicative scheme is worse by AUROC.
evidence_items.title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: What a Hallucination Benchmark Measures, and What It Does Not A Format-Controlled Audit of Structural Classification

evidence_items.summary: Learning-based distribution system state estimation (DSSE) predictors trained with the squared loss estimate the conditional mean of the state given the measurements. Under contaminated measurements, the conditional mean shifts, and the unbounded influence of the squared loss allows a few corrupted samples to dominate training. We replace the squared objective with the Gaussian kernel modal loss Lb(r)=1−exp(−r2/(2b2)), whose influence is bounded and redescending and whose population minimizer converges to the conditional mode as the bandwidth b→0. The mode-seeking formulation admits a learning-theoretic analysis: the population risk minimizer converges to the conditional mode as b→0; the score is bounded and redescending; a Rademacher bound of order O(1/n) controls generalization; the clean risk under Huber εc-contamination exceeds the optimal clean risk by at most 2εc+4Γn; and nonconvex SGD converges with bandwidth-controlled gradient variance. Experiments follow a corrected, seed-disciplined protocol (independent training runs, train-only normalization, paired corruption realizations, bootstrap confidence intervals) on four systems: CIGRE-14, IEEE-30, Oberrhein-70, and the independently generated external PanTaGruEl IEEE-14 benchmark. The modal-loss multilayer perceptron attains significantly lower voltage RMSE than its squared-loss counterpart at every tested condition on all four systems, with paired-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. In a comparison against conventional robust losses, no statistically detectable difference was found between the modal loss and the Tukey biweight under the tested configuration, while the modal loss outperformed MSE and Huber (δ=1.0) at the frozen parameter values; the modal objective replaces a finite residual cutoff with a smooth bandwidth parameter.
evidence_items.title: Mode-Seeking Kernel Losses for Robust Distribution System State Estimation: Contamination-Stability Theory and Cross-System Evidence

evidence_items.summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in military decision-making and operational systems, developments that take a rigorous and mission-oriented approach to adversarial assessment are necessary. To this end, this research introduces an Agentic AI Red Teaming Framework for the military domain that is designed to capture the security and safety robustness together with the operational trustworthiness of AI systems. It does so by adopting a socio-technical and Systems of Systems (SoS) approach in conditions of uncertainty across four layers: goal and profiling, adversarial scenario generation, execution, and impact assessment which enables a systematic progression from threat identification to mission-level consequence analysis. To this end, the framework is including an attack taxonomy which is further instantiated on AI-enabled DSS (Decision Support Systems) and AWS (Autonomous Weapon Systems) use cases across the process lifecycle that includes phases such as threat modelling and assessment. Through this framework, the research contributes to the development of responsible and trustworthy military AI systems that account for human–AI teaming, operational constraints, and governance obligations under conditions of uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI red teaming framework in the military domain

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language model (LLM) based agents are moving from executing well-specified tasks to Agentic Design: shaping what and how to build upstream of fabrication, integration, and deployment. However, an internally coherent but externally infeasible design propagates its compounding error downstream. The failure is easy to overlook, yet consequential and hard throughout: a design-generating loop rarely includes a check against the world, and the error surfaces only after the artifact is built. Design Grounding names the correspondence between such a design and the world it must satisfy. The mechanisms that establish it exist in adjacent fields but have been introduced into the design loop only in isolated, domain-specific forms, which leaves the same difficulty scattered across fields under different names. Studying both sides through their own corpora, the review is the first to consolidate them into one unclaimed problem. What makes the problem hard is structural: a design's referent is a system that has not been built, and the model that produces the design cannot supply it without external intervention. The review is exploratory in aim: it characterizes the problem and screens Agentic Design and Grounding in all four combinations. Reading titles and abstracts with an LLM flags roughly one in fifteen of nearly three thousand papers as closing the Design Grounding loop; only twenty survive full-text adjudication and manual review. Those twenty sort into four structural difficulties, and each becomes an open problem whose parts already exist in an adjacent field but remain unassembled.
evidence_items.title: Introducing Grounding into the Agentic Design Loop: An Exploratory Review of an Unclaimed Problem

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems extend language models with planning, memory, tool invocation, data access, and autonomous action, creating enterprise capabilities that also expand the security boundary beyond prompt-response applications. This review examines how prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory manipulation, and excessive agency threaten agentic workflows across finance, healthcare, software development, customer operations, and critical business services. It analyzes direct and indirect prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved documents, webpages, emails, databases, and multimodal content, emphasizing how untrusted instructions can override policy or redirect plans. Tool poisoning is examined through malicious descriptions, compromised connectors, deceptive outputs, dependency tampering, and excessive permissions that enable unauthorized data access or transactions. The review further evaluates memory attacks through false fact insertion, persistence abuse, cross-session contamination, sensitive-data retention, and retrieval manipulation. Excessive agency is framed as a control failure arising when agents possess broad objectives, inadequate constraints, irreversible tools, or weak human oversight. Defensive approaches include instruction-data separation, contextual trust labeling, least-privilege authorization, capability-based tool access, schema validation, content sanitization, provenance tracking, memory partitioning, transactional safeguards, runtime policy enforcement, and human approval for consequential actions. Detection methods combining behavioral telemetry, execution graphs, anomaly scoring, canary resources, and policy-violation monitoring are compared using attack success rate, false alarms, intervention latency, task utility, and operational cost.
evidence_items.title: Securing Agentic AI Enterprise Workflows Against Prompt Injection Tool Poisoning Memory Manipulation and Excessive Agency Threats

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) by reducing authoring costs and enabling flexible interaction. However, effective tutoring requires more than fluent responses. It also depends on pedagogical control, domain grounding, learner modeling, interaction design, orchestration, and reliable evaluation. We examine these requirements through a component-centric framework that organizes LLM-based tutoring systems into four functional layers: pedagogical policy, domain and grounding, learner state, and interaction/interface. A cross-cutting orchestration layer coordinates these components, while agentic tutoring systems are treated as an emerging subset of the broader field. Drawing on representative literature on LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems, published mostly between late 2022 and mid-2026, we analyze how tutoring capabilities are implemented across system architecture, learner modeling, interaction, orchestration, and evaluation. The reviewed literature suggests that evaluation remains concentrated on response-level and model-based proxies, while direct evidence of learning gains remains limited. Learner-state modeling and interaction design also receive less systematic attention. We conclude by identifying challenges in answer leakage, pedagogy–solving trade-offs, learner-state calibration, interaction validity, and proxy validity.
evidence_items.title: What makes an LLM a tutor? A component-centric survey of LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) may support structured extraction from clinical free text, but evaluation should consider accuracy, output validity, and inference efficiency. Objective To evaluate LLM performance–efficiency trade-offs in Chinese clinical text extraction across model scale, reasoning mode, temperature, architecture, and text-only versus multimodal configurations. Methods This single-center retrospective benchmark sampled 100 Chinese clinical reports per task: left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) extraction, carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) extraction, and coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA) classification. The same 300 reports were evaluated under 23 conditions, yielding 6900 outputs. Outcomes included output validity and all-report accuracy (exact-match for LVEF and IMT; classification for CTA). Class-specific precision, recall, and F1, macro-F1, and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) were calculated among valid CTA responses. Local inference efficiency measures included tokens, time to first token, and end-to-end latency. Results Four designated default configurations achieved 99.7% overall accuracy and 100.0% validity. CTA accuracy was 99.0%, with valid-response macro-F1 of 0.984–0.985 and MCC of 0.969–0.970, although false-positive and false-negative errors differed. Reasoning increased Qwen3-0.6B overall accuracy from 31.0% to 88.7% and CTA MCC from 0.025 to 0.599. For Qwen3-32B, overall accuracy increased from 98.7% to 99.7%, CTA MCC from 0.890 to 0.970, and median end-to-end latency from 3.746 to 32.097 s. Temperature changes offered no consistent improvement across CTA metrics. Dense and mixture-of-experts configurations had closely spaced CTA metrics but different latency and token profiles. Text-only and multimodal Qwen configurations showed no consistent relative advantage across two temperatures.
evidence_items.title: Performance–efficiency trade-offs of large language models for structured extraction from Chinese clinical free text: a benchmark study of model scale, reasoning mode, and architecture

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding in radiology and digital health; however, their diagnostic performance across diverse clinical scenarios and fine-grained visual reasoning tasks requires systematic evaluation. Objective The study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and fine-grained visual reasoning performance of 5 multimodal LLMs with bilingual medical imaging questions. Methods This cross-sectional benchmark study evaluated bilingual medical imaging questions using zero-shot prompting on 5 LLMs: GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Doubao, Yuanbao, and Llama 4 Maverick. Subgroup analyses by language (English/Chinese), question type (image/text), imaging modality (computed tomography, radiography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, and nuclear medicine), and anatomical system (neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, genitourinary, and musculoskeletal) evaluated intermodel accuracy and intramodel consistency. Image-based visual reasoning performance was assessed across modality, anatomy, lesion detection, and localization. Results A total of 298 questions (198 image-based, 100 text-based) were evaluated. Gemini 3 Pro achieved the highest overall accuracy (n=268, 89.9%, 95% CI 86.0%‐92.9%), significantly outperforming Doubao (n=235, 78.9%; P <.001), GPT-5.2 (n=233, 78.2%; P <.001), Yuanbao (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001), and Llama 4 Maverick (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001). All models performed better on text-based than image-based questions (Yuanbao, P <.001; Doubao, P =.02; GPT-5.2, P <.001; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.002; Llama 4 Maverick, P <.001).
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Fine-Grained Image-Interpretation Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models on Bilingual Radiology Questions: Cross-Sectional Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for temporal knowledge graph completion (temporal KGC), but accuracy alone does not reveal dependence on historical context. We evaluate Normal, No History, Anonymous, and Noisy evidence conditions on ICEWS14 and ICEWS18 with four instruction-tuned LLMs. We also test Temporal Evidence Filtering (TEF), a deterministic, training-free proof-of-concept selector combining relation compatibility, temporal recency, and entity-role consistency under a fixed ten-fact prompt budget. Removing or displacing history lowers accuracy; Anonymous improves it but simultaneously changes the constrained candidate vocabulary, precluding a single-mechanism explanation. TEF has positive descriptive differences in all 24 dataset–model–metric contrasts. Across eight dataset–model pairs, its equal-weight macro Hits@10 gain is +0.031375 (nominal paired-bootstrap 95% confidence interval: [+0.021875, +0.040875]); 10 of the 24 individual contrasts remain significant after Holm correction. Qwen3-4B selector baselines, component ablations, parameter sensitivity, and a disjoint second query sample qualify this result. TEF adds a mean 4.360 and 19.071 ms of CPU selection per query on ICEWS14 and ICEWS18, respectively; it does not compress the Normal prompt or establish an end-to-end speedup. Conclusions concern tail prediction with constrained generated lists on these two datasets, not exhaustive ranking or an identified internal reasoning mechanism.
evidence_items.title: Temporal-LLM-KGC: A Diagnostic Study of Temporal Evidence in Large Language Model Knowledge Graph Completion

evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of medical large language models (Med-LLMs) demands reliable, reproducible, and clinically relevant evaluation protocols. Existing paradigms, including rule-based metrics, expert evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge, suffer from semantic coverage gaps, high cost, inconsistent scoring, and judge bias. We propose a Consensus-Aligned Elo (CA-Elo) framework integrating: (1) a three-level hierarchical indicator system covering diagnostic capability, clinical usability, and trustworthiness, weighted via Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) from public and medical expert perspectives; and (2) an adaptive Elo update scheme with learnable dynamic K-factors, soft labels, and batch consensus anchors. Experiments on 1,000 HealthBench QA samples across four Med-LLMs show CA-Elo preserves perfect ranking while improving score stability and cross-batch reproducibility, offering a practical, low-bias solution for standardized Med-LLM benchmarking.
evidence_items.title: A consensus-aligned Elo evaluation framework for medical large language models

evidence_items.summary: Objective To evaluate the performance of GPT-5.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Pro in automated breast cancer cTNM and AJCC anatomic staging from Chinese-language PET/CT reports. Methods A curated test set of 298 pretreatment 18 F-FDG PET/CT reports from routine clinical practice, obtained between February and December 2025 at our institution, was included. All reports had been verified against the corresponding imaging findings and screened to exclude errors or omissions. Following AJCC 8th-edition cTNM criteria, GPT-5.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Pro assigned cT, cN, cM, and AJCC anatomic stage using a task-specific, rule-guided zero-shot prompt developed using a separate set of 20 reports and locked before final evaluation. Model outputs were compared with an expert report-based reference standard. Performance against this reference standard was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 score; agreement was assessed using Cohen's κ. Model errors were categorized as diagnostic reasoning, feature processing, or knowledge application errors. Results For cT staging, GPT-5.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Pro achieved accuracies of 98.3% and 97.0% ( P = 0.39) and macro-F1 scores of 0.968 and 0.952 ( P = 0.51), respectively. For cM staging, the corresponding accuracies were 99.7% and 98.0% ( P = 0.06), and the macro-F1 scores were 0.990 and 0.932 ( P = 0.06). cM1 sensitivity was 96.3% versus 77.8%, with 1 versus 6 missed cM1 cases, respectively. A significant performance difference emerged in cN staging, where GPT-5.5 Pro achieved higher accuracy (97.3% vs. 87.2%, P &lt; 0.001) and macro-F1 score (0.959 vs. 0.729, P &lt; 0.001), resulting in superior overall AJCC anatomic stage classification (accuracy, 98.3% vs. 90.3%; macro-F1, 0.968 vs. 0.861; both P &lt; 0.001). Agreement with the reference standard was almost perfect for GPT-5.5 Pro across all tasks ( κ = 0.96–0.98), whereas κ values for DeepSeek-V4-Pro ranged from 0.80 to 0.95.
evidence_items.title: Automated breast cancer staging from Chinese-language PET/CT reports using two large language models: a retrospective single-center study

evidence_items.summary: Egocentric video reasoning capability is essential for advancing the development of first-person wearable devices. However, most existing egocentric video understanding tasks are limited to single-instance text input, overlooking the model’s capability to reason about context throughout the entire duration of the video. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel task named Egocentric Video Dialogue, which refers to answering questions by considering both the video content and dialogue history. To support this task, we design a new dataset, EgoDialogue, which constructs continuous dialogues based on video question answering datasets. Egocentric videos and dialogue histories present two challenges, requiring the model to understand core interactions in visual data and the dialogue history in text, respectively. To address these issues, we introduce an EgoReason framework, consisting of an interaction exploration module and a dialogue reasoning module. The former module first reorganizes patches that correspond to the same spatial position across different frames and then sorts these blocks according to their frame order. In this way, it models spatiotemporal dynamics to help explore interactions. The latter module improves the understanding of dialogues by gradually integrating the questions and answers from each dialogue round into the fusion layer. In the experiments, our method shows superior performance compared to several VideoQA models and vision language models, achieving state-of-the-art results in prediction accuracy and various machine translation metrics.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Egocentric Video Dialogue: A Contextual Reasoning Approach with New Benchmark Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Training reactive machine learning potentials (MLPs) requires extensive quantum chemical labeling of nonequilibrium configurations along reaction pathways, motivating the use of data from lower levels of theory through pretraining and Δ-learning. However, whether combining these strategies consistently improves accuracy and downstream performance remains unclear. Here, we benchmark direct and residual training, each with and without pretraining, across DPA-2, DPA-3, MACE, and DPA4-Neo, using 17.6 million configurations labeled with GFN2-xTB and 198,622 configurations labeled at the ωB97X-D/def2-TZVP level. With the full DFT training set, pretrained Δ-learning achieves the lowest energy or force MAE averaged over three training seeds in 31 of 32 combinations of architecture, data set, and property. Learning curves for DPA4-Neo nevertheless show that direct finetuning reaches the MAE of a model trained from scratch on the full data set using no more DFT training configurations than pretrained Δ-learning in all eight combinations of data set and property, while avoiding repeated GFN2-xTB evaluations during inference. Pretrained Δ-learning also improves reaction energies and forward barriers across all four architectures on GDB-10-rxn and reduces median Hessian eigenvalue errors for the evaluated DPA4-Neo checkpoint. However, local force errors can remain incompletely corrected, and these improvements do not consistently increase the success rates of reaction search workflows initialized from specified reactant and product geometries, indicating that the preferred protocol depends on the data budget, target property, and downstream workflow.

evidence_items.summary: Spoofing and layering, in which orders are placed without intent to execute and canceled after influencing prices or visible liquidity, threaten market integrity, and fixed-threshold surveillance rules struggle to separate them from legitimate high-frequency trading. This paper proposes a machine learning framework for real-time spoofing and layering sur-veillance. The framework combines order-level, cancellation, trader-level, order-book, and temporal features; compares rule-based, supervised, ensemble, sequential, and anomaly-detection models; and specifies performance measures including precision, recall, false-alert rate, latency, and explainability. Because labeled spoofing data are not public, the evaluation protocol is exercised on a semi-synthetic benchmark: 183 hours of real BTC-USD order-book snapshots from a public exchange feed, with injected and labeled spoofing episodes. On a chronological test period, supervised models improved only modestly on a rule-based baseline (F1-score about 0.14 versus 0.10) and with low precision (at most about 0.12, against a base rate of about 0.03). Ensemble models did not outperform logistic regression, and detection depended strongly on episode intensity, from 21% to 45% of low-intensity episodes to 76% to 87% of high-intensity episodes. The results show that the protocol can be executed and give a first reference point, not evidence of operational readiness.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning for Spoofing and Layering Detection in Real-Time Market Surveillance: A Framework and a Semi-Synthetic Order-Book Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Enterprises now build many agentic applications on Large Language Models (LLMs), yet a large share of these efforts stall before dependable production, and the cause is rarely raw model capability (Brown et al., 2020; Bommasani et al., 2021). The cause is an engineering one. Agent prototypes tend to couple the parts that rarely change, such as graph topology and module boundaries, with the parts that change often, such as prompts, thresholds and decision policies, so a small behavioural request forces edits across the codebase and erodes the trust that production demands (Parnas, 1972; Sculley et al., 2015). This paper presents a reference framework for building agentic systems as a disciplined engineering practice. The framework rests on three contributions. First, a four-phase lifecycle (define, design, develop, deploy) gives a repeatable path from a framed problem to a running service. Second, a structure-behaviour separation principle splits a frozen scaffold and a canonical specification from a versioned runtime configuration, and pairs a no-code behaviour loop with a gated evidence-to-code loop, so most change is resolved without touching structure. Third, a multi-plane execution model separates an orchestration plane over a typed shared state, a communication plane with a typed message contract, and a tooling plane with a uniform invocation interface, above a governed data-product substrate. A capability and operating-model dimension and a five-level maturity model accompany the framework. A conceptual synthesis was followed by a small expert appraisal, in which practitioners rated change-locality and governance fit favourably (M = 5.8, SD = 0.7, on a seven-point scale). The findings suggest that treating structure and behaviour as distinct change surfaces, under typed orchestration and evidence-driven evaluation, may raise the share of agentic pilots that reach reliable operation, warranting cautious generalisation beyond the appraisal sample.
evidence_items.title: Specification-Governed Agentic Systems: A Lifecycle and Multi-Plane Reference Framework for Enterprise Multi-Agent Engineering

Dataset accompanying the paper Sycophantic Metacognition: Investigating the Dunning-Kruger Effect in Large Language Model Self-Assessment , ACM Conversational User Interfaces 2026 (CUI '26) ( https://doi.org/10.1145/3816046.3816233 ). Paper abstract. As large language models are deployed in conversational settings where users calibrate trust against model-reported confidence, the reliability of that self-report becomes a central question for conversational user interface design. This paper introduces sycophantic metacognition, the production of confidence outputs that mimic the surface form of metacognitive judgment without any operational process linking them to accuracy. Drawing on Model Dependent Ontology, we identify a double unmooring in LLM self-assessment, arising from the simultaneous absence of an operational ground linking confidence to accuracy and a stable self-model accumulated across interactions. The framework yields four falsifiable predictions, supported by experiments spanning six LLMs, four domains, three difficulty levels, and multiple pressure conditions. Confidence tracks the surface form of authority rather than evidential content, and we derive concrete design implications for conversational interfaces. Known limitations. Verbalized confidence is treated as a model output, not as evidence of internal confidence states. evidence_items.summary: Overview and motivation This deposit provides a reproducible compilation of high-redshift luminosity-function measurements and pragmatic combined constraints derived from them. Published luminosity functions at the same nominal redshift are often inconsistent within their quoted statistical uncertainties. Differences can arise from sample selection, photometric-redshift inference, completeness corrections, contamination, galaxy-AGN classification, host-galaxy subtraction, dust treatment, survey volume, cosmic variance, gravitational-lensing models, and assumptions used to convert observed counts into number densities. Selecting a single measurement can therefore make model calibration or inference depend strongly on one survey. This compilation instead retains the visible disagreement among datasets and constructs a broad empirical summary suitable for model comparison, forecasting, and exploratory inference. Data products The deposit contains an executed and documented Jupyter notebook and three machine-readable JSON files: The [O III] galaxy luminosity functions cover \(z=6,7,\) and \(8\). The rest-frame ultraviolet galaxy luminosity functions ( GLF UV ) cover \(z=5,6,7,8,9,10,13,\) and \(15\). The rest-frame ultraviolet quasar/AGN luminosity functions ( QLF UV ) cover \(z=5,6,7,8,9,\) and \(10\). The notebook includes two embedded figures showing the original literature measurements, upper limits, combined mean curves, and shaded uncertainty regions. Upper limits are plotted for all three observables but are not included in the combined constraints. Role of astrodatapy The literature measurements are retrieved using astrodatapy , a Python package that maintains a curated collection of published observational and modelling results and exposes them through a common programmatic interface.

evidence_items.summary: The Projection-Reality Divergence Persistence Theory (PRDPT) is a proposed cognitive-systems framework for investigating whether and how a prior projection continues to influence post-event processing when an observed or verified outcome substantially departs from that projection. The motivating claim is broader than the persistence of a belief: a prior projection may influence attention, evidence selection, evidential weighting, causal attribution, interpretation, memory, belief updating, decisions, behavior, or subsequent projections, even when the person or system ultimately revises its original position. The framework distinguishes the actual event from accessible evidence, prior projection from realized outcome, residual influence from projection-consistent belief persistence, and ordinary interpretive continuity from demonstrable cognitive bias. Its default mechanism is the Reality-Divergence-Triggered Projection Carryover Mechanism (RDPCM). Its primary case is the Contrary-Reality Projection Persistence Case (CRPPC). The manuscript defines a construct registry, divergence taxonomy, operational measurement strategy, Bayesian normative comparator, Projection-Aligned Carryover Index (PACI), candidate subjective-updating model, and dynamic state-transition framework. It also specifies information-theoretic measures, cross-domain research roles, falsifiable hypotheses, rival-model comparisons, research-design requirements, and an A-Z manuscript-production roadmap. PRDPT is presented as a research proposal rather than a verified universal law. Related work on belief perseverance, biased assimilation, misinformation correction, and evidence evaluation provides a relevant research context, but does not establish that a single carryover mechanism operates in every person, task, or computational system. The framework's novelty, parameter validity, causal interpretation, predictive advantage, and cross-domain invariance must be established empirically.
evidence_items.title: THE PROJECTION-REALITY DIVERGENCE PERSISTENCE THEORY (PRDPT)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: This paper introduces the Criterion-Reflexive Reconfiguration Theory (CRRT), a proposed general framework for investigating situations in which an evaluative criterion, governing rule, assumption, or decision procedure becomes an object of higher-order examination. The theory addresses how such examination may produce an independently significant realization, justify a revision of the original criterion, change subsequent classifications, or leave the original evaluation unchanged. The theory's primary case is the Meta-Level Lesson-Emergence Case (MLEC): an individual recognizes that not every thought constitutes an important lesson and then recognizes that this distinction may itself constitute an important lesson. The case illustrates a general structural relationship between evaluating an object and evaluating the criterion by which that object is assessed. The generalized theory is not restricted to thoughts, learning, or metacognition. The paper defines a canonical terminology, seven foundational axioms, six principal propositions, a ten-stage default mechanism, a cross-level outcome taxonomy, a mathematical modeling schema, candidate application domains, falsifiable hypotheses, counterexamples, and a staged empirical research program. It distinguishes meta-level significance emergence from criterion revision, ordinary reclassification, and strict interpretive reversal. Formal expressions are used to specify the proposed relationships; they are not presented as empirical proof. The central contribution claimed here is a proposed integration of criterion-as-object examination, independent assessment of the resulting realization, conditional reclassification, and feedback-based criterion updating within a single analytical architecture. Its distinctiveness relative to existing theories, empirical adequacy, and domain generality remain open research questions.
evidence_items.title: The Criterion-Reflexive Reconfiguration Theory (CRRT)

evidence_items.summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On τ^2-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.
evidence_items.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.
evidence_items.title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference

evidence_items.summary: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves 1.32times-2.42times validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.
