evidence_items.summary: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.
evidence_items.title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.
evidence_items.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Visual speech recognition (VSR), which transcribes speech from lip movements alone, offers a privacy-preserving and noise-robust communication channel for assistive healthcare: it enables silent speech interfaces for post-laryngectomy and intubated patients, hands-free documentation for clinicians in sterile environments, and confidential voice-free communication in shared wards. Despite this promise, the application of large language models (LLMs) to VSR postprocessing remains underexplored, and prior LLM-based rescoring studies have largely treated hyperparameters as fixed rather than systematically optimized. We present a systematic empirical study of LLM-enhanced VSR along two dimensions: (1) a comparison of decoder-based LLM generation against N-best semantic re-ranking under matched computational budgets; and (2) a grid-search optimization of the re-ranking hyperparameters—candidate-list size N and acoustic/semantic fusion weights (α, β). On three benchmarks (CMLR, LRS3, and CN-VSRC), the proposed re-ranking approach consistently outperforms both the baseline VSR decoder and decoder-based LLM generation. Optimized hyperparameters yield a character error rate (CER) of 6.73% on CMLR, a word error rate (WER) of 28.62% on LRS3, and a CER of 14.68% on CN-VSRC, corresponding to relative improvements of 16.08%, 12.05%, and 18.80% over the respective baselines. These results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic re-ranking is a practical, training-free, and deployment-friendly post-processing module for assistive healthcare communication systems.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-enhanced visual speech recognition for assistive healthcare communication

evidence_items.summary: Legible robot motion should reveal the intended goal early while remaining collision-free and reasonably short. Under a small function-evaluation budget, however, continuous trajectory search leaves little room to discover intent-expressive motions through optimization alone. Standard population optimizers typically begin with random candidates, which provide numerical diversity but no scene-specific guidance for communicating intent. We evaluate a three-prior protected-greedy design under a shared low function-evaluation budget. We propose Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization (PPG-LLM-GWO). One structured large-language-model query returns confusion-aware, early-discrimination, and corridor-handling priors; after deterministic geometry repair, these trajectories occupy the three initial GWO leader roles, and 17 feasible-random trajectories complete the population. Subsequent sweeps protect the entering leaders, update only ordinary wolves, accept only feasibility-first improvements, and re-rank all survivors. We evaluate the method on a 24-map development bank at BFE∈{50,150}, using batch-aligned area under the best-so-far curve (AUC) after population initialization as the primary metric. Against original GWO, the development mean differences are +0.00222 [−0.00076, 0.00508] and +0.01040 [0.00543, 0.01616], respectively. The interval includes zero at BFE=50 but is above zero at BFE=150; PPG-LLM-GWO has the largest batch-aligned mean among the tested population optimizers at both settings. At BFE=50, the paired AUC differences versus PSO, DE, and GA are +0.02621, +0.01529, and +0.03349, respectively, with all three intervals above zero. At BFE=150, the differences are +0.01721, +0.02565, and +0.04954, respectively, and all four intervals, including the comparison with GWO, are above zero.
evidence_items.title: Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization for Low-Budget Legible Motion

evidence_items.summary: This study examines whether large language models (LLMs) can perform audit work by comparing their performance with human learners, across model scale and under two enhancement techniques. Drawing on the audit-judgment distinction between declarative and procedural knowledge, the study evaluates seven publicly available LLMs on audit work in two forms of audit assessment. In the knowledge-based assessment, the LLMs answer four undergraduate auditing examinations previously sat by 352 accounting students, as a proxy of human learners. In the data-analytic case assessment, they plan and execute SQL-based substantive procedures to test the occurrence of revenue and the completeness of expenditures. On the knowledge-based assessment, LLMs outperform human learners where large LLMs typically fall between the 78th and 98th student percentiles, and large LLMs outperform small LLMs. On the data-analytic case assessment, no LLM scores above 50% of the rubric maximum, and large and small LLMs do not differ significantly. Meanwhile, two enhancement techniques: self-reflection and agentic workflow do not improve performance on the data-analytic case assessment. These results reveal a knowing–doing gap: LLMs display strong declarative audit knowledge but weak procedural capability, and self-correction without external feedback does not repair knowledge errors. This study discusses implications for audit practice, assessment design and standard setters.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models In Auditing Assessments: Comparisons Between Human Learners, Model Scale, and Enhancement Techniques

evidence_items.summary: To address the issues of insufficient professional knowledge and low accuracy in question answering within the field of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) using general-purpose language models, this paper proposes a method for constructing a TCM question-answering model by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model. First, relevant TCM literature and diagnostic knowledge are collected and organized to construct a domain-specific question-answering dataset, achieving a structured expression of TCM knowledge. Second, instructions are fine-tuned on the pre-trained language model to adapt it to question-answering tasks within the TCM domain. Finally, experimental validation is conducted in TCM consultation and knowledge-based question-answering scenarios, and the model is compared with the non-fine-tuned model. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively improve the accuracy and professionalism of the model's question-answering in the TCM field, demonstrating its potential value for intelligent TCM consultation applications.
evidence_items.title: Research on fine-tuning and application of domain-specific large language model for traditional Chinese medicine consultation

evidence_items.summary: This study presents a prototype for the structured analysis of PubMed case-report titles, keywords and abstracts, combining domain fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and five specialist-role agents with a synthesis agent. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B was fine-tuned using QLoRA on 8999 reports with teacher-generated targets. The retrieval index contains 7679 chunks from 13 medical sources. On 501 held-out reports, symmetric final-answer-only scoring, with missing final answers assigned zero, showed increases after fine-tuning in ROUGE-1 (+0.0253, 95% CI +0.0107 to +0.0394) and structural completeness (+0.0371, +0.0160 to +0.0579). The mean BERTScore difference was +0.0035 (−0.0085 to +0.0153), providing inconclusive evidence of a mean improvement. Among the tested platform configurations, retrieval showed no clear benefit on the reported final-answer reference metrics, and the specialist panel scored below a single structured agent. Final-answer results for the full platform versus the model alone were mixed. The full platform used 11.7 times as many tokens and 5.9 times the latency of the fine-tuned model alone. A blinded LLM-as-a-judge audit of 1941 statements found that 20–24% were unsupported or contradicted by the supplied sources; among checkable factual statements, this proportion was 24.5–28.5%. Different report requirements and a shared 1024-token generation limit constrain component-level interpretation. The results concern the evaluated configurations, reference similarity, format and source agreement; they do not establish improved diagnostic accuracy or clinical safety.
evidence_items.title: A Fine-Tuned Multi-Agent Large Language Model Platform with Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Clinical Case Report Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Online consumer reviews encode rich signals about brands, yet converting this unstructured text into actionable positioning insight remains challenging. This study proposes an LLM-driven framework that extracts structured brand perception variables from e-commerce reviews and demonstrates it in the headphone category. Using an analytic file of 5,895 review-level observations covering Sony, Bose, JBL, and Beats, we employ a structured GPT-5.4 prompt to extract multidimensional brand perception indicators from each review, capturing associations, judgments, emotional attachment, advocacy, and attribute focus. A manual validation exercise based on 400 stratified reviews showed meaningful agreement between the LLM-coded outputs and an adjudicated human benchmark. The results reveal clear brand separation. Bose leads on perceived quality (4.20/5), recommendation rate (78.3%), and strong emotional connection (39.9%), whereas Sony achieves the highest value perception (3.97/5). Beats and JBL occupy weaker quality positions, though Beats retains a comparatively stronger emotional profile. Patterns in attribute emphasis also help distinguish the brands: Bose reviews are distributed across sound quality, active noise cancellation, and comfort; Sony reviews emphasize sound quality, comfort, and value; JBL reviews are heavily concentrated around sound quality; and Beats reviews emphasize sound quality, value, and design. Negative reviews provide additional diagnostic insight, revealing durability and fit issues for JBL and perceived value concerns for Beats. The study contributes primarily to LLM-assisted marketing analytics and applied brand diagnosis by showing how constrained and human-validated LLM coding can transform review text into a scalable, multidimensional brand monitoring instrument. Brand equity and positioning theory are used as conceptual foundations for organizing the extracted perception variables rather than as targets of theoretical extension.
evidence_items.title: Mapping headphone brand positioning from e-commerce reviews with large language models

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: The aim of this study was to evaluate how three artificial intelligence (AI)-based neonatal seizure detectors (NSDs) perform in a large, clinically acquired data set and their potential to support timely seizure identification. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of continuous EEG (cEEG) recordings from 169 neonates born at ≥35 weeks gestation with neonatal encephalopathy. Seizure presence was determined by independent review by two or three pediatric encephalographers, and 2,455 individual seizures were annotated by a single expert as a pragmatic, clinically representative reference standard. Three NSDs were evaluated: a feature-based support vector machine detector (NSD1) and two deep-learning detectors (NSD2 and Persyst-15). Using an any-overlap approach, outcomes included neonate-level seizure identification, seizure-level detection, false detections per day (FD/day), and detection latency. Results: We analyzed 15,343 hours of cEEG (median 98 hours per neonate); 55 neonates (33%) had seizures. All NSDs identified ≥95% of neonates with seizures. Seizure-level detection varied: NSD2 detected 35% (IQR 17–53%), NSD1 63% (IQR 38–82%), and Persyst-15 60% (IQR 37–80%) of seizures. NSD1 generated significantly more FDs (46 FD/day, IQR 22–82) than NSD2 (3.2 IQR 1.2–9.3) and Persyst-15 (2.8 IQR 1.1–6.2; P < 0.0001). The median time to first true detection was <1 minute for NSD1 and Persyst-15, versus 26 minutes for NSD2. Conclusions: AI-based NSDs demonstrated high infant-level sensitivity but different tradeoffs between seizure-level detection and alarm burden. These findings highlight how AI tools may augment clinical EEG workflows and support earlier seizure recognition, while underscoring the need for evaluation under real-world conditions to guide safe and effective implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Neonatal Seizure Detection: A Pragmatic Evaluation of Clinical Performance Tradeoffs in Clinical EEG

evidence_items.summary: The placenta is a crucial determinant of the success of pregnancy. However, manual evaluation of its pathology is limited by poor reproducibility and a global shortage of specialized perinatal pathologists. Besides, predicting recurrent pregnancy complications remains highly challenging, which severely limits the timely deployment of proactive therapeutic interventions. Automated artificial intelligence screening of the delivered placenta will help to overcome these bottlenecks. In this work, we synthesize the transition toward self-supervised Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) that yield robust, stain-agnostic tissue embeddings. Furthermore, we evaluate the emergence of Non-Euclidean Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that map cellular topologies to quantify mal-perfusion, alongside multimodal generative cross-attention networks (MGCN) that integrate gigapixel histology with electronic medical records (EMR) to improve pregnancy risk stratification. Moreover, we propose a novel, functional systems-biology framework to retroactively bridge digital morphometrics – such as impaired trophoblast fusion and invasion – to upstream dysregulated molecular cascades, including the ERK1/2–DUSP, FAK–MAPK, and HIF-1α regulatory axes. Finally, we address translational bottlenecks – such as diagnostic inter-observer variation, systemic clinical confounders, and geographic data bias – and outline hardware edge-deployment strategies for the pathology floor. Ultimately, automated placental screening will help to reveal immediate newborn developmental risks and maternal pathological recurrence risks across subsequent pregnancies. Together, these computational paradigms offer a potential translational roadmap to standardize digital placental pathology into a personalized reproductive medicine pillar.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Placental Pathology: From Spatial Analytics to Molecular Proxies

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Aflatoxin contamination in peanut is highly variable across the growing season and may differ among seed fractions and locations within a field. Understanding its temporal dynamics, environmental associations, and spatial heterogeneity is essential for developing targeted aflatoxin risk-assessment and management strategies. This study aimed to characterize temporal, environmental, and spatial patterns of aflatoxin contamination in larger and smaller peanut seed fractions across commercial rainfed fields in Georgia and to evaluate the ability of environmental variables to predict contamination and deviations from expected seasonal patterns. Repeated in-season sampling was conducted in five commercial rainfed peanut fields. Sampling time was standardized using days after planting (DAP). Statistical inference, nonlinear seasonal modeling, and machine-learning analyses were integrated to evaluate seed-fraction differences, characterize seasonal contamination trajectories, and identify environmental predictors. Model performance was assessed using nested cross-validation with inner-fold hyperparameter optimization, permutation importance, TreeSHAP analysis, and leave-one-field-out validation. Spatial visualization was used to characterize within-field contamination heterogeneity across sampling events. Seed-fraction differences were seasonally dependent, with significantly greater contamination in the smaller fraction during middle sampling events but no significant differences at the beginning or end of the sampling period. Environmental prediction was stronger for direct contamination than for deviations from expected in-season trajectories. The best models explained 27.1% and 41.6% of direct-contamination variability in the larger and smaller fractions, respectively, compared with 10.9% and 18.6% of in-season-deviation variability.
evidence_items.title: In-season Patterns and Environmental Drivers of Aflatoxin Contamination Across Peanut Seed Size Fractions

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background Contamination of serum samples with the anticoagulant potassium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (kEDTA) constitutes a critical pre‐analytical error in veterinary diagnostics and can lead to potentially life‐threatening misinterpretation of biochemical test results. Objectives To develop and validate a method for quantifying EDTA in canine and feline sera. A second aim was to evaluate the effect and prevalence of kEDTA contamination in canine and feline serum samples. Methods A copper‐PAN‐based automated method for quantifying EDTA in canine and feline sera was developed. Canine and feline serum samples admitted together with EDTA tubes were analyzed for kEDTA contamination. Results The measuring range was set to 0.03–0.4 mM, with a coefficient of variation of < 13.1% and acceptable linearity upon dilution (75%–118%). Spiking experiments demonstrated that kEDTA caused a dose‐dependent increase in potassium and decreases in calcium, magnesium, iron, and zinc, with iron and zinc most profoundly affected. The allowable total error was exceeded at low kEDTA concentrations, even when analytes remained within reference intervals. A prevalence study of 1065 serum samples submitted with kEDTA tubes revealed contamination rates of 1.1% in dogs and 1.8% in cats. Conclusions These findings emphasize that even small amounts of kEDTA can compromise diagnostic accuracy. This underscores the importance of strict compliance with recommended blood collection order and highlights the value of direct EDTA measurements in veterinary laboratory diagnostics.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The contamination of water by heavy metals is a great concern for many countries worldwide because of their potential to harm human health and biota. Although bordered by a mosaic of conservation units, the Amapari River (Brazil) is impacted by legal and illegal mineral exploitation. However, data on metal concentrations and related risks remain scarce. This study aimed to evaluate the concentrations of Cr, Cu, Fe, Hg, Ni, Mn, Pb, and Zn in Amapari River water and to assess compliance with environmental and drinking-water standards. We also calculated the Risk Indexes (RI), Chronic Daily Intake (CDI), Risk Quotients (RQ), and Carcinogenic Risk (CR) for ingestion and dermal pathways. Cr, Cu, Fe, Ni, Mn, Pb, and Zn were quantified using flame atomic absorption, and Hg was measured with hydride generation coupled to ICP-MS. Pb, Cu, and Hg exceeded CONAMA 357, and Pb exceeded Ordinance 888. The mean CDI values for ingestion were higher than those for dermal exposure for all analyzed metals. RQ values for ingestion were greater than those for dermal contact. RI was 3.03, showing the potential for adverse noncarcinogenic effects on human health. CR values for Pb and Cr through ingestion were both above 10–4, reflecting a high risk of cancer. CR values for dermal exposure to both metals were also above 10–4. This study demonstrated that the Amapari River is contaminated by multiple metals and poses potential risks to human health. These findings highlight the urgent need for environmental monitoring, regulatory enforcement, and mitigation measures.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In this work, we present the results of an investigation into low-frequency seismic noise in an underground laboratory infrastructure, serving as a case study for the future Einstein Telescope. Specifically, we focus on the low-frequency noise measured at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso, LNGS), expanding upon previous findings at the same location. Finally, we estimate upper limits on the expected tilt noise, considering only the ground contribution (i.e., without considering any other contributions from specific experimental setup), for frequencies below 70 mHz, using seismic data from LNGS and KAGRA. Finally, these underground upper bounds are superimposed and compared directly with the official active seismic isolation requirements of the Einstein Telescope. Our findings confirm that the ambient underground tilt levels comply with ET suspension control targets, providing vital engineering guidance for active tilt-attenuation strategies in next-generation gravitational-wave observatories.
evidence_items.title: Estimation of an upper limit on ground tilt noise in an underground research infrastructure as a benchmark for the Einstein Telescope

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence agents—software systems that perceive, reason, plan and act over multiple steps with limited human intervention—are moving from research prototypes towards clinical deployment. Recent reviews map what has been built; this one asks what would have to hold for such systems to be deployed safely. We conducted a scoping review reported according to the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, searching eight bibliographic sources from January 2017 to June 2026, admitting foundational computer science and regulatory literature alongside clinical applications. Five architectural paradigms recur—tool-augmented large language model agents, multi-agent systems, offline reinforcement learning agents, embodied robotic agents and autonomous monitoring agents—nearly all sharing a common four-layer stack. We introduce a six-level scale of clinical agent autonomy that grades systems by where human judgement enters relative to the reasoning, and by whether the resulting action remains reversible. The scale exposes an inversion in the evidence base: demonstrated patient benefit concentrates at high autonomy in narrow, bounded domains, whereas research effort concentrates at intermediate autonomy, where prospective outcome evidence is absent and automation bias is the dominant risk. We further propose seven evaluation dimensions specific to agency, a mapping of evaluation requirements to autonomy level, and a ten-item failure mode taxonomy assigned to the architectural layer at which each is addressable. Deploying agentic systems safely requires prospective multi-site validation, reporting standards adapted to agency, equity-aware design, and regulatory obligations indexed to autonomy rather than algorithm class. We conclude with an eight-point research agenda.

evidence_items.summary: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.
evidence_items.title: PolyRoute: A Twelve-Language and Code-Mixed Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing, with Baselines and a Leaderboard

evidence_items.summary: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.
evidence_items.title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control

evidence_items.summary: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.
evidence_items.title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model

evidence_items.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/prh-closer-look.
evidence_items.title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis

evidence_items.summary: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.
evidence_items.title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module

evidence_items.summary: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to sim10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.
evidence_items.title: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Human cognitive tasks let us compare language models with humans under controlled conditions. Yet a model can reproduce the direction of a human effect while making different errors. CogBattery evaluates 54 open-weight language models on text adaptations of 13 cognitive paradigms, comparing each with human data from its source study. Like humans, models respond more to n-back lures than to controls, yet they make far more false alarms on ordinary non-targets. Most models' reported confidence separates correct from incorrect answers less well than humans' does, and most always choose the same wager, including models that classify accurately. These patterns span many model families. Across tasks, model scores share two dimensions. The first is closely tied to scale, yet larger models are not consistently closer to humans. Predefined cognitive groupings show no reliable predictive advantage over random groupings of the same size. These results show that matching human effect directions does not establish human-like behavior. CogBattery provides condition-level human references for testing errors and confidence reports in new models.
evidence_items.title: CogBattery: Human-Referenced Evaluation of Cognitive Task Behavior and Structure in Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.
evidence_items.title: WMIP: A Working-Memory-Inspired Programmable Probe of Cumulative State Tracking in Large Language Models
